items.title: Explaining and interrupting collective misalignment in language model systems
items.content: arXiv:2611.11724v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: In collectives, language model agents can exchange individually innocuous messages that together support a policy violation. Understanding and preventing collective misalignment requires answering the question of which messages sufficiently influenced and necessarily enabled the violation. Collective Dependence Analysis (CDA) operationalises necessity and sufficiency to explain decisions and find the fewest removals interrupting support within tested combinations. Tests covered constructed violations, unscripted agent conversations, and recorded interactions, with selected message removals reducing violations from 93% to 6% in controlled cases. Using O(N) model evaluations for N messages, CDA achieves the same violation reduction with half the deletions of a frontier LLM judge given the transcript and asked for all supporting messages in eligible operational cases. CDA also proposes the mechanism through which the collective misalignment emerged. Nonetheless, complete explanations remain difficult on unfamiliar tasks and some removals can inadvertently disrupt correct decisions. CDA unifies explanations of collective misalignment with experimentally tested interventions.

items.title: AbductionBench: Benchmarking Abductive Reasoning in Large Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.10705v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Abductive reasoning is the inference of plausible explanations for observed evidence. Evaluating this capability requires more than a single task: a system may need to generate an explanation, discriminate among competing hypotheses, revise its hypotheses as evidence arrives, or decide what evidence to seek next. Yet these capabilities are typically evaluated through isolated benchmarks with different task formulations and scoring procedures, so claims that a model is ``good at abduction'' may reflect only a narrow aspect of this capability. We introduce AbductionBench, a unified framework whose taxonomy characterizes abductive tasks. We instantiate this framework on 27 datasets spanning ten domains and evaluate eight LLMs from four model families evaluated on single-choice selection tasks. Beyond harmonizing heterogeneous tasks, AbductionBench separates final-answer evaluation from analysis of the observable reasoning traces and interaction histories produced alongside those answers. We analyze written traces as observable model outputs rather than faithful representations of internal computation, characterizing evidence use, hypothesis comparison, uncertainty, contradiction handling, and answer commitment. Jev matches or exceeds small LLMs when selecting among explanations over compact evidence but falls substantially behind on longer cases, suggesting that candidate discrimination and extended evidence integration place different demands on a system. In interactive tasks, the proportion of actions judged relevant declines at later steps, and a relevant first question is associated with a correct final answer; in the passive task, models rarely revise their initial hypothesis as new evidence arrives. Together, these findings highlight the value of evaluating abductive reasoning through both final answers and observable evidence use, hypothesis revision, and information gathering.

items.title: Efficient Online Submodular Maximization with Bandit Feedback
items.content: arXiv:2611.11808v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We study online monotone submodular maximization under a cardinality constraint with bandit feedback. On each round, the learner selects at most $k$ elements from a ground set of size $n$ and observes only the value of the selected set. We develop an efficient algorithm achieving $O\!\left(k\sqrt{nT\log(n/k)}\right)$ expected $(1-1/e)$-regret over $T$ rounds. To our knowledge, this is the first polynomial-time algorithm with $\sqrt{T}$ dependence on the horizon for arbitrary monotone submodular functions in the bandit setting. Our approach uses randomized sampling and a carefully constructed potential to reduce online submodular maximization to online linear optimization over the probability simplex.

items.summary: The paper gives the first polynomial-time algorithm for online monotone submodular maximization under a cardinality constraint with bandit feedback that achieves expected (1-1/e)-regret with a square-root horizon dependence. The approach uses randomized sampling and a potential-based reduction to online linear optimization over the probability simplex.
items.reasoning: A clear algorithmic milestone in online learning theory, claiming the first efficient square-root-regret algorithm for this general setting, with rigorous analysis from a credible optimization and theory group.

items.title: NCCL-BOT: Closing the Loop on NCCL's Cost Model with Online Bandits
items.content: arXiv:2611.11303v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: NCCL picks an algorithm-protocol pair for every collective from an analytic cost model (AUTO) that never sees a measured latency. The model is a strong prior but a brittle final decision: priced on forced-arm runs, its choice is exact on most contexts and badly wrong in a few. We built NCCL-BOT, a tuner plugin that closes the loop: a per-context bandit, warm-started from the model, learns from measured latencies. We replay a forced-arm H100 sweep, tuned at 4-8 nodes and scored at 16-32, and price the model's choice on the same forced arms; that sweep has no stock-NCCL run. The bandit cuts the contexts where the model's choice loses more than 10% from 19 to 1 (p99 103% to 9.9%, mean 6.1% to 1.6%; p=0.047 over nine scenarios after Holm correction). The prior and continued learning both matter: cold-started bandits, and committing after one probe of each arm, lose more on the mean in every scenario. Supervised selectors fit once on the same data and tuned with the same budget match the mean, and their heavier tail is not significant (7 against 1 contexts above 10%, p=0.06); at seen scales they match or beat online selection. With hyperparameters frozen from H100, UCB1 cuts AUTO's p99 from 60% to 23% and from 56% to 15% on two GB200 fabrics, but its contexts above 10% go from 16 to 8 on one and from 10 to 13 on the other, and scenario-level tests do not separate the two. Live, on two latency-emulated node sets of one H100 system with one run per policy, the learners repair most of a gross AUTO error on one (selection loss 31% to 6-8% for deterministic Greedy and UCB1; average all-reduce bandwidth 1.18-1.24x stock) but average 0.94-0.99x stock on the other, and on both lose to stock below 1 MiB (on the first through plugin overhead); on H100 the cost model is exact there offline, so small sizes can be left to it. We do not show a net end-to-end win.

items.title: Nonasymptotic causal structure learning in generalized linear DAGs with continuous optimization
items.content: arXiv:2611.11667v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We study the problem of learning directed acyclic graphs from observational data in nonlinear models and provide finite-sample, nonasymptotic statistical guarantees in these models. Although widely studied, statistical guarantees for gradient-based methods in nonlinear models are missing from the literature. Under a generalized linear model for each node, we analyze a global nonsmooth objective combining an exact acyclicity constraint with a quasi-minimax concave penalty, which can be optimized via standard gradient-based solvers. We establish finite-sample guarantees under this model, including the most widely used logistic and Poisson models. Experiments corroborate structure recovery accuracy and computational performance, including both standardized data and negative controls as baselines.
items.author: Chang Deng, Inbeom Lee, Bryon Aragam
items.summary: This paper provides finite-sample, nonasymptotic statistical guarantees for gradient-based learning of directed acyclic graphs in nonlinear generalized linear models, including logistic and Poisson cases. It analyzes a global nonsmooth objective combining an exact acyclicity constraint with a quasi-minimax concave penalty. This fills a notable gap, since statistical guarantees for gradient-based DAG methods in nonlinear settings were previously missing.
items.reasoning: Theoretically substantive contribution to causal discovery, a foundational area, closing a well-identified gap between widely used continuous-optimization DAG methods and their statistical guarantees. Solid methodology and experiments, though it is a focused theoretical extension rather than a broad breakthrough.

items.title: Planners Exploit Deterministic Error: Dithered Low-Bit World Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.11780v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Sampling-based planners such as MPPI and CEM query a learned world model thousands of times per control step, so low-bit world models are an obvious way to make model-based control cheaper on a robot. With round-to-nearest activation quantization and no calibration, we find that planning can collapse, by up to 100 points of success, while the world model's latent one-step prediction error stays no larger than that of a stochastic rounding scheme that plans well. At the same bit width, what decides the outcome is not the size of the rounding error but whether it persists across planner iterations and is shared across candidates. Round-to-nearest leaves an error that persists, and an iterating planner drifts toward the candidates that this error favors; in TD-MPC2, holding the same dither fixed within a step or an episode brings the drift back. Dither shared by all candidates and redrawn at every iteration removes most of the damage at the same bit width and without training: at least half of it in all 19 affected Meta-World cells (task $\times$ bit width) of TD-MPC2 (median 95%), in 4 of 5 DINO-WM cells, and in all 8 affected tasks of a 317M-parameter multi-task TD-MPC2. Captured as CUDA graphs on an Ampere GPU, a W8A4 integer TD-MPC2 world model runs its planning rollouts 1.9-3.3$\times$ and the whole planning step 1.3-1.5$\times$ faster than FP32, though not faster than BF16 with pre-converted weights; shared dither adds at most 2.3% latency. In TD-MPC2, block-scaled NVFP4 removes most of the damage and MXFP4 part of it, which ties the failure to coarse grids with a shared scale. Hypotheses, thresholds and analysis code were fixed before the data that test them, and the hypotheses that failed are reported.
items.author: Yong Hwi Song, Keon Myung Lee
items.summary: This paper studies low-bit quantized world models for sampling-based planners like MPPI and CEM, showing that with round-to-nearest quantization planning can collapse by up to 100 points of success even though one-step prediction error is small. The deciding factor is not error magnitude but whether the error persists across planner iterations and is shared across candidates. Dithering with stochastic rounding prevents this systematic drift.
items.reasoning: A sharp, actionable insight for efficient model-based control: deterministic quantization error systematically biases iterating planners even when standard error metrics look fine. Clear empirical findings with direct implications for deploying quantized world models on robots; methodology is focused but well-executed.

items.title: WorkflowArena: Benchmarking Executable Workflow Orchestration in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
items.content: arXiv:2611.12856v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly deployed as multi-agent systems rather than as a standalone model operating within a single context. Recent agent harnesses allow the model to instantiate worker agents and to author the executable workflow that coordinates them, shifting the design of system structure from developers to the model at run time. The quality of this organization therefore constitutes a distinct capability, yet existing benchmarks either measure end-to-end task completion or evaluate coordination under structures specified in advance. We formalize this capability as workflow orchestration and introduce WorkflowArena, a benchmark of 145 long-horizon tasks spanning 8 professional domains, from software engineering and formal mathematics to legal analysis and 3D production. Each task specifies an initial workspace and an integrated deliverable composed of interdependent components, which is assessed by a hidden verifier. Agents determine autonomously whether and how to delegate, and all delegation is recorded, enabling joint evaluation of deliverable quality and the organization of the underlying work. Experiments with nine models show that no single configuration performs best across all domains and that systems exhibit distinct delegation strategies: at high effort, Claude models in Claude Code invoke workflows less frequently but with larger worker groups, whereas GPT models in Codex delegate more frequently in smaller units. When the executing model is held fixed on a challenging subset of tasks, workflows authored by Claude Opus 5.5 substantially improve weaker executors, indicating that workflow organization is itself a measurable determinant of task performance.

items.title: Beyond AUROC: Deployment-Aware Evaluation of Model-Internal Jailbreak Detectors
items.content: arXiv:2611.11067v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in user-facing systems, where jailbreak attacks can bypass safety controls and induce harmful and policy-violating outputs. Recent model-internal detectors use hidden representations, gradients, or internal signals to identify such prompts, but their practical security value depends critically on behavior at low false-positive operating points rather than on area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) alone.   We study two data dependencies that shape this behavior: calibration data, which determine the detection threshold, and reference data, which can influence detector scores. Across four model-internal detectors, four LLMs, and twelve jailbreak families, thresholds calibrated on curated benign prompts frequently fail to preserve their false-positive rate (FPR) budgets on real-user traffic. Recalibration improves false-positive control but reveals substantial family-level coverage gaps, including cases with high AUROC but low true-positive rate (TPR). Causal reference-set interventions show that changing reference composition can substantially alter family-level detection and that improving coverage of one attack family can reduce coverage of others.   These findings show that calibration and reference data are part of a detector's security behavior. We therefore recommend evaluating model-internal jailbreak defenses using realized FPR on deployment-like traffic and per-family TPR at explicit low-FPR operating points, with AUROC used as a complementary ranking metric rather than the primary security measure.

items.title: Map2SLAM: From Streaming Map Prediction to Real-Time SLAM
items.content: arXiv:2611.11169v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Streaming 3D foundation models (3DFMs) estimate camera poses and dense geometry online, but they fall short of SLAM: their predictions are fixed once emitted, so loop closures cannot correct accumulated drift. With such models already providing strong geometric capability, a central question for SLAM becomes how to schedule their inference and how to keep its results as revisable state. We present Map2SLAM, which keeps LingBot-Map frozen, trains only a lightweight retrieval head, and builds SLAM on the model's inference interface, turning its predictions into observations of an external persistent SLAM state. The front-end tracks every incoming frame with the model's causal streaming inference and decides which frames are written to the persistent state as keyframes. The back-end asynchronously decides when and which past frames to re-observe, re-running the model's joint inference over them with fresh context; verified loop observations correct the trajectory online, and segment observations refine dense geometry after the sequence. All invocations share a single frame encoder pass per image, whose cached features also drive loop retrieval, so frequent re-invocation incurs no additional encoding cost. Map2SLAM achieves state-of-the-art performance on KITTI, VBR, and Oxford Spires, reducing mean ATE by over 40% compared with the best uncalibrated baselines, while maintaining real-time tracking at over 28 FPS at a resolution of $518\times154$ on an NVIDIA RTX 5090D GPU. Please visit our project page at https://robbyant-research.github.io/Map2SLAM/.

items.title: EditJudge-Bench: Auditing VLM Image-Edit Judges with Synthetic Ground Truth
items.content: arXiv:2611.12524v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used as automated judges for image-editing benchmarks, yet their reliability is poorly understood. Auditing these judges is difficult because real edited images lack controlled ground truth and entangle the requested changes with model artefacts, unintended side effects, and ambiguous degrees of success. In this paper, we introduce EditJudge-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark of 1,382 synthetic before/after image pairs rendered in Blender, with edits parameterised across nine categories derived from real user requests and exact ground truth from known 3D scene parameters. Because every edit is generated by a known intervention on a controlled scene, EditJudge-Bench evaluates VLM judges as binary verifiers of whether an instruction was correctly executed, isolating judge perception from editor quality. Across 25 judge configurations, we find substantial reliability gaps: (a) the widely adopted VIEScore template reaches only 69.0% AUROC with GPT-4o; (b) fine-tuned judges score 51.7-66.3%; spatial edits such as rotation and shape remain challenging; (c) prompt-formatting choices like image-text ordering shift performance by up to 14.1 points. Despite using only synthetic data, judge rankings on EditJudge-Bench correlate strongly with two real-image human-preference benchmarks ($\rho$=0.95 and $\rho$=0.71), indicating that controlled audits surface failure modes relevant to real evaluation.

items.title: VLA-MOPD: On-Policy Distillation for Multi-Task VLA Policy Consolidation
items.content: arXiv:2611.12286v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Physical intelligence requires embodied agents to ground language in observations and execute actions while retaining useful skills. Vision-language-action (VLA) policies offer a shared interface, but task-specific post-training often produces separate specialists. Consolidation is difficult: mixed-task reinforcement learning provides sparse trajectory-level credit, while offline distillation may miss student-visited observations and endpoint distillation does not supervise intermediate action-generation states. We introduce VLA Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (VLA-MOPD), a protocol for consolidating flow-matching VLA specialists. After acquiring task or suite experts, a shared student collects robot rollouts and queries the instruction-routed frozen teacher at each visited observation and intermediate ordinary differential equation (ODE) state. Detached per-flow-step transition targets supervise valid action chunks through a masked local matching loss; an optional reference-policy term supports retention on other tasks. Starting from one trajectory per LIBERO task, VLA-MOPD raises mean success-once from 75.4% to 98.9%, compared with 98.15% for endpoint action distillation. It improves mean RoboTwin 2.0 success from 73.0% to 89.3%; on a Piper robot, two consolidation rounds improve average success from 70.0% to 90.0%. In a near-matched Spatial-adaptation study, reference matching limits the Object suite decrease to 3.0 points, versus 13.2 without the reference term.

items.title: ObjectWorld: Scaling Object-Centric World Models with A Large-Scale 3D Full-Object Flow Dataset
items.content: arXiv:2611.11085v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Generative world modeling from large-scale visual data offers a promising path toward scalable robot manipulation. This calls for an intermediate representation that can be supervised at scale and remains actionable for downstream control. We propose 3D full-object flow, an object-centric motion representation that assigns dense 3D trajectories to points across the complete surface of a target object, including its occluded regions. By extending visible-surface object flow to the full object geometry, this representation makes complete object motion explicit and applies uniformly to both rigid and deformable objects. To realize the potential of this representation at scale, we introduce a 1210-hour full-object flow dataset that addresses the scarcity of large-scale supervision for complete 3D object motion. The dataset integrates diverse real-world videos and physical simulations, with a scalable annotation pipeline for recovering full-object motion from real-world observations and quality metrics for systematically assessing annotation quality. We then train a world model that takes an image and a task description as input and predicts dense full-object flow over the reconstructed object geometry. Experiments show reliable annotation quality, data-scalable flow prediction, and effective downstream manipulation across novel scenes and robot embodiments. Project website with additional results and videos: https://nus-lins-lab.github.io/ObjectWorld/.

items.title: Flip Anything with Agentic Robotics Self-Learning
items.content: arXiv:2611.11941v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Flipping is a fundamental robotic manipulation skill that requires reorienting a target object in a stable pose on a planar support surface by rotating it 180$^\circ$ about an axis parallel to the support surface -- think of flipping a coin from heads to tails. Although flipping is a common objective in industrial tasks such as parts inspection, mechanical assembly, and tool use, coding a bimanual robot with grippers to flip diverse objects is a significant challenge. In this paper, we show that a coding agent can autonomously develop and refine object-flipping strategies through iterative learning in physics simulations across diverse object geometries. Progressive skill acquisition, from basic handover to toppling and pushing, robust grasping and sensing, and thin-object manipulation with recovery, improves task success from 24.7% to 95.0%. The resulting graph-based code integrates high-level strategy selection with reactive control, enabling multi-stage flipping on physical robots.

items.title: Restoring General and Improving Domain-Specific Safety in Fine-Tuned LLMs Without Retraining
items.content: arXiv:2611.10279v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Safety-aligned language models are known to suffer degradation in refusal behavior following domain-specific fine-tuning, even when the fine-tuning data is entirely benign. The predominant mitigation strategy, preference optimization on the fine-tuned model, is computationally expensive and requires domain-specific preference data that is often unavailable in practice. We propose SPECTRA, a training-free, weight-level method that restores refusal behavior by transferring the base model's refusal direction into the fine-tuned model's weights via an activation-aware, low-rank update, requiring no gradient-based optimization or domain-specific safety data. The low-rank design restricts the intervention to the subspace most causally active on harmful inputs, leaving benign behavior largely undisturbed by construction. Empirically, SPECTRA substantially improves refusal behavior across a comprehensive safety evaluation, while preserving general coherence, domain-specific knowledge, and producing negligible change in false refusal rates.

items.title: Represented but Not Used: Value-Policy Dissociation in LLM Agents
items.content: arXiv:2611.10457v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents need to choose actions whose consequences unfold over multiple future steps, yet poor decisions do not reveal whether the model failed to represent those consequences or failed to use them. Mechanistic interpretability has studied internal representations of environment state and plans, but sequential decision making also requires evaluating how candidate actions change future outcomes. Reinforcement learning formalizes this as action value. We study this computation in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, and GPT-OSS-20B across a partially observed Grid environment and WebShop, a simulated web shopping environment. We find that the relative values of candidate actions are linearly decodable from intermediate hidden states, including at states where the policy prefers a worse action. We call this gap between value representation and policy choice value-policy dissociation. To investigate how represented value relates to action selection, we compare direct interventions along the value readout direction with Natural Value Transport (NVT), a transformation learned from hidden state changes that naturally result from differences in action value. While readout-direction interventions have limited and inconsistent effects, NVT more consistently influences action preferences, particularly at later layers. We also test a closed-loop controller that uses the value readout as a sensor and NVT as an actuator, observing improvements in task outcomes. These results suggest that LLM agents can represent useful prospective value without reliably translating it into policy choice.

This value-policy dissociation separates representation failures from usage failures. It matters for understanding why capable models make poor multi-step decisions.

items.title: Safeguarding Agentic AI in Radiology Workflows: A Multimodel Evaluation of Rule-based and Large Language Model-based Verification
items.content: arXiv:2611.11541v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Purpose: To estimate how often tool-using large language model (LLM) agents record clinically relevant false or unsupported information in simulated radiology documentation and how much safeguards applied before each action reduce these errors.   Materials and Methods: In this simulation study (October 2026), 48 synthetic, radiologist-reviewed base scenarios covered finding communication, tumor board preparation and follow-up management. Forty-three also had a misleading-information variant (91 variants). Six LLM agents (Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6.1-Sol, GLM-5.3, MiniMax M3, Gemma-4-31B, Qwen3.8-27B) completed each variant with permissions only, deterministic rules, and rules plus a locally run LLM checker (1638 episodes). The primary outcome was at least one executed high-severity violation per episode. Risk differences were estimated per agent at base-scenario level and, exploratorily, pooled across agents, with analyses of document access and blocks.   Results: With permissions only, 7.3%-27.1% of episodes had a high-severity violation (pooled across agents, 19.4%). Pooled, it was 16.7% with rules (-2.8 percentage points; 95% CI: -6.1, 0.5) and 13.2% with rules plus the LLM checker (-6.2; 95% CI: -9.5, -3.0). Adding the LLM checker to rules changed it by -3.5 (95% CI: -6.3, -0.7). No difference between agents was detected (P = .43), and task success did not decrease detectably. In misleading variants, agents opened the altered document in 83% of episodes regardless of error, and 58% of erroneous statements cited it. Most blocked actions (64%-68%) would not have caused a violation and were returned for revision.   Conclusion: Layered safeguards reduced but did not prevent high-severity errors. Errors after misleading information reflected misjudged rather than missed information.

items.title: Causal Signal Credit Assignment for Verilog Code Generation via Counterfactual Hardware Verification
items.content: arXiv:2611.11848v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large language models have improved Verilog generation, yet functional correctness remains difficult to optimize because simulation commonly provides a coarse module-level pass/fail outcome. Such feedback discards useful evidence from partially correct RTL modules and cannot determine whether a source statement is functionally responsible for an observed output behavior. We present a new method named Causal Signal Credit Assignment (CSCA), which is a counterfactual preference-optimization framework for Verilog generation. CSCA first performs continuous signal-level behavioral verification on sampled candidate modules. It then locates output-driving assignment spans and applies five interventions while holding the remaining module and testbench fixed. The resulting changes in signal-level errors are combined with behavioral agreement to form a continuous statement credit, which is mapped to response-token weights for strict weighted direct preference optimization. This enables CSCA to learn from locally supported statements without uniformly reinforcing an otherwise incorrect response. Built on Icarus Verilog and a CodeV-derived corpus, CSCA is evaluated on VerilogEval~2.0 and RTLLM~v2.0, including both code completion and specification-to-RTL tasks. With a Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct backbone, CSCA leads the evaluated 7B-scale models and remains comparable to the much larger GPT-5.4-mini on the reported Verilog-generation benchmarks.

items.title: Learning to Act with World Models by Valuing What Comes Next
items.content: arXiv:2611.12200v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: A sparse terminal reward tells an agent little about its steps. Much of the missing information is implicit in the environment's dynamics, because each state transition can change the conditions for success long before the reward arrives. A world model trained on real transitions can learn to predict what each action changes, but a predicted observation does not by itself show whether success has become more likely. With a binary terminal reward, PPO's critic makes this judgment by estimating the current policy's probability of success, but only for states the agent reaches. Our method, WM-PPO, elegantly brings the two together. For each action the policy samples, executed or not, the world model predicts the next observation and the critic values the predicted successor. In the policy channel, comparisons among these values give the policy auxiliary advantages; in the value channel, their mean gives the critic an auxiliary target. A shared gate weights both channels according to how reliably comparisons with similar margins predicted real outcomes earlier in training. The policy, critic and world model all learn from the agent's own interaction, with no teacher or privileged information, and only the policy is used at inference. With a comparable number of real environment steps, WM-PPO raises success from PPO's 63.5% to 87.5% on ALFWorld and from 39.3% to 52.9% on ScienceWorld. It matches the strongest PPO refinements we tested on ALFWorld and exceeds the best of them by 6.5 points on ScienceWorld. The trained policy more often completes prerequisite steps before placing an object or committing to an answer.
items.author: Chenghao Gao, Zhi Zhang, Dian Jin, Yihe Pan, Doudou Zhou
items.summary: WM-PPO combines world models with PPO so that for every sampled action, executed or not, the world model predicts the next observation and the critic evaluates whether that transition improves the probability of eventual sparse terminal reward. This extracts dense learning signal from environment dynamics without requiring reward-shaped environments.
items.reasoning: Using imagined next states to densify sparse-reward credit assignment is a clean, well-motivated idea with clear connections to model-based RL, and the theoretical framing of valuing transitions rather than observations is elegant. It competes with a large body of prior model-based RL methods.

items.title: Shortcuts and Boundaries: Verifiable RL Misalignment and Contextual Safety Learning
items.content: arXiv:2611.12865v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve an agent's task capability while reinforcing behavior that violates contextual execution requirements. We study this reward-driven misalignment, including reward hacking, through verifiable reward--context conflicts, where compliant task completion remains feasible while some executable shortcuts earn more reward than every compliant strategy. Encoding these conflicts in task dynamics lets us generate diverse interactive environments at scale and derive compliance feedback from execution histories. In resource and reporting workflows, task optimization increases real productivity through unauthorized resource use or raises reported scores while actual work declines. Controlled changes in the training distribution show that minority conflict exposure can still lead to widespread shortcut acquisition, reaching 97.9\% certified profitable violations on an API task under a 25\% conflict mixture after 128 updates. The same contextual checks supply a simple binary penalty that supports joint capability and compliance gains and partially mitigates acquired violations. Learned safety adapts to expanded authorization and transfers across mechanisms into workflows with evolving evidence and approval requirements. On 32 unseen changing-evidence tasks, resource-trained safety increases safe completion from 53.1\% to 89.1\% relative to task-only training, while both policies achieve full real work. These results connect a verifiable account of reward-driven misalignment with scalable task construction and safety learning that remains useful under changing execution requirements.

items.title: Efficient Learning of Differentiable MPC Policies on the GPU via Smoothed ADMM and First-Order Reinforcement Learning
items.content: arXiv:2611.09937v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Differentiable model predictive control (MPC) enables structured, constraint-aware policies to be optimized end-to-end. However, learning MPC policies faces two bottlenecks: (1) nonsmooth sensitivities at active-set transitions and (2) expensive policy evaluation, since each requires an optimization solve. We first introduce SmoothedTurboMPC, a GPU-parallel differentiable MPC solver combining sequential quadratic programming (SQP) with a log-barrier-smoothed alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) inner solver. Its design enables smooth gradients, exact sensitivities at convergence, and efficient execution on GPUs. Second, to efficiently train MPC policies, we pair our solver with first-order reinforcement learning (FORL) using Short-Horizon Actor-Critic (SHAC), which reuses rollout MPC solutions instead of repeatedly re-evaluating them. Comparisons with state of the art solvers show that the approach achieves up to $4.4\times$ higher end-to-end training throughput. On a vehicle racing task, our method achieves higher returns than MPC PPO with a $46\times$ speedup, training on 3.3 million transitions in only 7 minutes. Finally, we use the framework to train a more reliable MPC racing policy via RL with domain randomization, and validate it on a full-scale race car. We integrate our advances into the open-source TurboMPC solver.

items.title: Memory flows: geometry and dynamics of sequential retrieval in input-driven Hopfield networks
items.content: arXiv:2611.09995v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Associative memory models classically describe retrieval as convergence to stored patterns, but the theory of sequential retrieval remains comparatively limited. We develop a two-timescale input-driven Hopfield network in which fast associative retrieval is modulated by a slow feedback variable evolving over a prescribed memory-transition graph. This yields autonomous, graph-constrained transitions while preserving analytical tractability. Using slow-fast and geometric singular perturbation theory, we characterize memory fixation via memory manifolds and identify the geometric regions that govern stability loss and escape from retrieved memories. We further derive reduced slow dynamics and explicit criteria for transition onset, self-sustained retrieval, and collapse, expressed through escape times, gain thresholds, and fixed points. Together, these results provide a tractable framework for analyzing feedback-driven sequential retrieval in Hopfield networks.

items.title: Covariate-Conditioned One-Step Diffusion for Multi-Horizon 3D Brain MRI Prediction in Aging and Neurodegeneration
items.content: arXiv:2611.10043v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Predicting longitudinal brain changes from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can help characterize structural progression associated with aging and neurodegeneration. However, diffusion-based forecasting typically requires iterative denoising, limiting inference efficiency. We propose a covariate-conditioned one-step diffusion framework for multi-horizon prediction of 3D gray-matter density (GMD) maps. Rather than directly generating future anatomy, the model predicts longitudinal GMD changes through residual prediction in a single denoising step. The predicted changes are added to the baseline GMD map to reconstruct future anatomy. The model is conditioned on baseline anatomy, age, diagnosis, APOE4 allele count, and continuous follow-up time. Training combines mean squared error with a Pearson correlation loss to improve the spatial agreement between predicted and observed GMD changes. A unified model supports prediction horizons from 2 to 10 years. On the held-out ADNI test set, our method achieves a $\Delta$-Pearson of 0.478, mean squared error (MSE) of $5.176 \times 10^{-3}$, and structural similarity index measure (SSIM) of 0.979, with $\Delta$-Pearson reaching 0.582 at 10 years. Without retraining, external evaluation on AIBL yields a $\Delta$-Pearson of 0.450, MSE of $4.016 \times 10^{-3}$, and SSIM of 0.985. Ablation studies further demonstrate the benefits of residual prediction, covariate conditioning, and correlation-based supervision. Code: https://github.com/natenaile/OneStepBrainMRI.

items.title: Can General-Purpose Generative AI Supply Training Data for Medical Vision Models? A Multimodal Retrospective Study
items.content: arXiv:2611.10484v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Background: Well-annotated, diverse medical imaging datasets remain a major constraint for vision-based medical AI. We evaluated Nano Banana, a general-purpose image generation and editing model, as a source of synthetic medical images for model training, subgroup augmentation, and model auditing. Methods: In this retrospective study across four imaging modalities, chest radiography, fundus photography, and CT models were trained only on synthetic images and externally validated on real-world data against real-data-trained models. Carotid ultrasound models were trained on a private Human Phenotype Project cohort (aged 40-75 years) with and without synthetic augmentation. Clinicians rated image plausibility. Evaluation used AUROC, AUPR, calibration, and decision curve analysis. Findings: Synthetic-only models achieved AUROCs of 0.877 (95% CI 0.843-0.910) for pneumonia (n=14863), 0.963 (0.948-0.975) for retinal detachment (n=1149), and 0.711 (0.600-0.823) for renal calculus (n=4122), comparable to real-data-trained models, but their calibration and net benefit were not consistently more favorable. With mixed synthetic-real training, a carotid ultrasound model produced an ordinal vascular age index that stratified 633 external subjects into subgroups differing in BMI and glucose (both p<0.01), linking vascular aging to cardiometabolic health. To stress-test shortcut learning, editing a moderate tessellated pattern into fundus photographs reduced the true-class probability for central serous chorioretinopathy from 0.996 to 0.822. Clinician-guided editing raised low-quality CT plausibility from 3.10/5 to 4.30/5. Interpretation: Synthetic data can complement real data in model training, subgroup representation, and model testing via controlled editing, but its clinical value should be assessed with calibration, decision curve analysis, and clinician review, not discrimination alone.
items.author: Jiachuan Peng, Kyle Lam, Jierui Qu, Lin Li, Haining Zheng, Bang Zheng, Aniruddha Agarwal, Zaki Almallah, Min Chen, Vicente Grau, Hagai Rossman, Eran Segal, Jianing Qiu

The results inform whether general generative models can substitute for scarce annotated medical imaging data. A timely empirical answer to a question of broad medical AI interest.

To stress-test shortcut learning, editing a moderate tessellated pattern into fundus photographs reduced the true-class probability for central serous chorioretinopathy from 0.996 to 0.822. Clinician-guided editing raised low-quality CT plausibility from 3.10/5 to 4.30/5. Interpretation: Synthetic data can complement real data in model training, subgroup representation, and model testing via controlled editing, but its clinical value should be assessed with calibration, decision curve analysis, and clinician review, not discrimination alone.

items.title: VisProve: Learning Typed Visual Provenance for Scientific Document Question Answering
items.content: arXiv:2611.10642v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Visual citations show where an answer is supported, but not how the cited content contributes to it. In scientific document question answering, a model may read a value directly, compress several observations, or combine evidence to infer a conclusion. We study typed visual provenance, where a system generates an answer together with source regions and explicit support relations. We introduce ReViE, a dataset of 3,941 questions over complete scientific documents, with page, section, and region annotations labeled as Quotation, Compression, or Inference. We further propose VisProve, which augments joint answer and provenance generation with differentiable Spatial Evidence Reading and Evidence-Answer Relation Feedback. VisProve conditions next-token prediction on localized visual evidence and its estimated support relation through a gated norm-bounded residual. On the document-disjoint ReViE test set, VisProve improves Typed-F1 from 3.52 to 5.48 and Section-F1 from 45.99 to 53.24 over joint supervised fine-tuning with the same backbone, while Page-F1 changes only marginally. These results suggest that coupling visual grounding with support relation modeling mainly improves fine-grained provenance, while the low absolute Typed-F1 reveals a substantial gap between answer generation and precise visual evidence attribution.

items.title: Behavioral Evaluation of Large Language Models Under Cognitive Biases in HAZOP Studies
items.content: arXiv:2611.10721v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Hazard and Operability (HAZOP) studies safeguard industrial processes against catastrophic accidents. Large language models (LLMs) increasingly assist HAZOP drafting, yet evaluations rely on lexical overlap. Because LLMs internalize human heuristics, prompts may trigger biased judgments. Whether frontier LLMs withstand cognitive perturbations in safety-critical workflows remains unknown. Here we show across 420 trials that three frontier LLMs resisted 96.8% of cognitive manipulations, rendering overall susceptibility statistically inconclusive. Contrary to assumed broad fragility, models rejected confirmation and availability cues. However, safety-critical risk downgrades emerged under low anchors and gain frames. Thus, automated hazard analysis requires disciplined human-in-the-loop validation.

items.reasoning: A well-designed empirical study on LLM susceptibility to biases in a safety-critical industrial workflow, with a nuanced finding (broad resistance but specific failure modes). Applied scope is narrow but the safety implications are concrete.

items.title: Statopia: A Prover--Library Ecosystem for Automated Formalization and Proof Discovery in Statistics
items.content: arXiv:2611.11110v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Theoretical results in statistics and machine learning rest on long, technically delicate proofs, and fluent arguments generated by large language models are not necessarily correct. Automated formalization makes such arguments mechanically checkable, and automated proving goes further by discovering machine-checked proofs for statements whose proofs are incomplete or missing altogether. Both require reconstructing assumptions from source materials, accessing specialized mathematical infrastructure and managing long proof developments. We present Statopia, an ecosystem that jointly develops Statopia Prover, an independent agent specialized for formalizing and proving results in statistics and machine learning, and Statlib, a Lean~4 library built with the prover and organized for automated use. The prover controls its own execution without relying on external coding agents. It is built for formal proof discovery and checking existing proofs. A natural-language proof, when available, guides its search but is not required: from a statement alone, the prover develops the argument itself and constructs a Lean proof. Its workflow integrates source preparation, statement review, library supported planning and proof construction. Dynamic proof dependency graphs and task groups support parallel, resumable proof development. Statlib's shared definitions and theorem interfaces are organized for retrieval and composition by agents, and its coverage of statistics keeps expanding. Verified results and usage feedback from the prover inform reviewed library updates, so that proof development drives this expansion. A cross-platform application provides an interactive workspace for uploading source files and running tasks locally or in the cloud.

items.title: Do Feature Interactions Break Explainability? Provable Explanations for Any-Order Neural Additive Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.11224v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Post-hoc explanation methods for neural networks are often heuristic and lack provable guarantees. A common alternative to such methods that was studied in recent years is to compute a cardinally-minimal subset of input features that is provably sufficient to determine the model's prediction. For general neural networks, however, finding such explanations is computationally intractable. In contrast, recent work showed that this problem becomes more tractable for a particular family of neural networks, namely neural additive models (NAMs), though standard NAMs are highly restrictive because they exclude feature interactions altogether. In this work, we study the computation of provably minimal and sufficient explanations for neural networks with restricted feature interactions, bridging the gap between fully general neural networks and purely additive models. We first prove that even with constant-order interactions, the problem is $\Sigma_2^P$-hard, implying that worst-case exponential complexity is unavoidable. We then identify two provably tractable settings: one based on sparsity in the interaction structure and another based on a stronger interaction-aware notion of sufficiency. Under either of these settings, we develop algorithms that compute provable explanations for neural networks with any-order interactions while retaining much of the computational efficiency of additive models. Empirically, we show that these explanations are significantly smaller and faster to obtain than those produced by standard algorithms, while being derived from models that achieve much higher accuracy than standard NAMs. Overall, our results help expand the class of neural networks that admit efficient provable explanations, while clarifying the fundamental role of feature interactions in shaping their complexity.

items.summary: Studies provably minimal and sufficient explanations for any-order neural additive models (NAMs with feature interactions), extending the tractability of provable explanations beyond standard NAMs which exclude interactions. The work provides formal guarantees for this family of networks.

items.title: Chatter Attack: Resource Consumption Attack for Large Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.11261v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: LLMs are powerful but incur substantial inference cost, which can be exploited by malicious users to induce overly long outputs, increasing latency and operational expense. Prior resource consumption attacks either coerce repetition or suppress the end-of-sequence token by lowering its logit value. However, with autoregressive, sampling-based generation, the search space grows exponentially with length and small deviations or unstable trajectories can derail optimization, limiting attack effectiveness and stability. To address this issue, we introduce Chatter Attack, a novel class of resource consumption attacks that optimize adversarial prompts to induce predefined short target phrases, thereby avoiding search-space explosion while still eliciting long responses. Specifically, Chatter Attack triggers self-doubt using short doubt-inducing phrases as the target, and sustains this state throughout generation via inference attention loss and global entropy loss. To extend to black-box settings, we further propose a novel Bayesian Prompt Optimization (BPO) method, which models the objective function globally by constructing a discrete token kernel, efficiently exploring the entire search space using prior information. Extensive experiments across multiple models and datasets show that our method outperforms baselines, with maximum response length increases to 31.5$\times$, and revealing practical resource-depletion risks for real-world LLM inference services.

items.summary: Introduces a resource consumption attack class that optimizes adversarial prompts to induce predefined short target phrases, which are then repeated to generate long outputs, avoiding the exponential search-space explosion of prior approaches that coerce repetition or suppress EOS tokens. The method improves attack effectiveness and stability in raising inference latency and cost.

items.title: How Much Training-Inference Mismatch Can On-Policy Distillation Tolerate?
items.content: arXiv:2611.11450v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model on its own responses, guided by a fixed teacher. Generating these responses is expensive, so systems use quantized inference and asynchronous rollouts to reduce the cost. Both, however, introduce training-inference mismatch between the rollout engine and the model being trained. Such mismatch can destabilize reinforcement learning (RL), but its effects on OPD remain unclear. This paper investigates how much mismatch OPD tolerates, where its effects arise, and how training systems can use this tolerance. Measuring all mismatch sources on one scale, we examine quantization across three student-teacher pairs, with additional tests of weight staleness and injected noise on one pair. OPD tolerates substantial mismatch without meaningful loss of training quality but degrades at higher levels, revealing an empirical mismatch budget. Both the quality cost of mismatch and the mismatch introduced by quantization depend on the model, with some layers particularly sensitive to reduced precision. In controlled comparisons, OPD remains stable under rollout configurations that destabilize RL methods. Under weight noise, mismatch also shifts the prefixes reached during generation, introducing errors that per-token corrections cannot address. To put these findings into practice, we introduce a lightweight admission check that screens rollout configurations against a calibrated budget without requiring a full training run for each candidate. Model-specific FP8 recipes preserve training quality while providing capacity for at least $1.93\times$ as many KV-cache tokens as BF16. Combining FP8 with asynchronous rollouts reaches the same training quality $1.62\times$ sooner than synchronous BF16 training. Code is available at https://github.com/benyucong/train-inference-mismatch-opd
items.author: Cong Yu, Ziting Wang, Songlin Jiang, Sitong Zhang, Chengliang Chai, Youhe Jiang, Eiko Yoneki, Tuo Shi
items.summary: This paper systematically quantifies how much training-inference mismatch on-policy distillation (OPD) can tolerate, covering quantization across three student-teacher pairs plus weight staleness and injected noise. It maps where mismatch destabilizes RL training and derives practical guidance for systems using quantized inference and asynchronous rollouts to cut costs.
items.reasoning: OPD is a practically important and fast-growing technique for post-training LLMs, and this is one of the first systematic studies of its robustness to the systems-level approximations (quantization, asynchrony) that real training stacks rely on. Solid empirical breadth and actionable systems findings, though the analysis is empirical rather than theoretical and limited to tested configurations.

items.title: Accelerated Reinforcement Learning for Soft Robotics: Hours Instead of Years
items.content: arXiv:2611.11718v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) requires large amounts of interaction data or a reliable simulator, both hard to obtain for nonlinear soft robotic hardware. Recent work shows that a time-scale separation inherent to soft robot dynamics justifies their reduction to low-dimensional invariant manifolds, known as adiabatic spectral submanifolds (aSSMs). We demonstrate that an aSSM-reduced model, a simple polynomial ordinary differential equation learned purely from pre-collected data, can serve as an RL training environment. On a pneumatically actuated soft arm, we train a trajectory-tracking policy in 3 hours on a six-dimensional aSSM-reduced model and deploy it without fine-tuning, whereas reproducing this policy training extrapolates to 3 years of hardware interaction. Our policy tracks dynamic targets with 40% lower error than otherwise identical policies trained on a 4.8-million-parameter recurrent neural network (RNN) or a 1.7-million-parameter transformer, which take 13 and 100 hours to identify, against 5 minutes for our mathematically justified 6,924-parameter model.

On a pneumatically actuated soft arm, a trajectory-tracking policy trains in 3 hours on the reduced model and deploys zero-shot, versus an extrapolated 3 years of training on the full-order system.

items.title: Text Alone Predicts Which Classes a Segmentation Readout Keeps
items.content: arXiv:2611.11926v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: An open-vocabulary segmentation readout silently loses a class deployed beyond its training categories. It still emits masks with high confidence, but the class never wins a single pixel. The training loss falls anyway, and mIoU can even rise while classes die. We show that which classes collapse is written in the class-name list alone. Before any image is seen, we rank each class's collapse risk from its text similarity to the training vocabulary alone. The ranking holds at AUROC 0.69-0.96 across nine model families, twelve backbones and eight pretraining recipes. Two further families, measured only after the predictions were written down, land in the same band. What the list writes, it can rewrite. With identical images and a class's counterpart moved in or out of the training list, retraining flips that class's gain over the frozen baseline by 21 IoU points; swapping in unrelated names changes nothing. We find a vocabulary-distance mechanism behind the collapse. Collapsed classes lose every vote to near-name neighbors, but in the frozen features they survive. Turning down the readout's amplitude, or stopping training early, brings them back, up to +16 points, without retraining; trained with its amplitude held down, the readout never collapses.

It also demonstrates that adjusting a class's coupling can revive collapsed classes with identical images.

items.title: The balance between feature learning and collapse in dynamical systems-based generative models
items.content: arXiv:2611.12156v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Over the past decade, a growing body of work has established that implicit biases in learning dynamics fundamentally shape the solutions found by neural networks, governing their learned features and generalisation performance. However, despite these strides in deep learning theory, far less is known about representation learning in generative models based on dynamical systems, from normalising flows to diffusion. Importantly, empirical evidence suggests that continuous-time generative models can be prone to mode collapse, yet a learning theory explaining such biases remains elusive. To address this, we use tools from dynamical systems and operator theory to express the gradient flow of a general class of stochastic differential equations as a composition of linear operators, allowing us to relate collapse to low-rank biases in generative models. In variational inference and flow-matching tasks, we show that this bias can manifest in two different mechanisms: i) where collapsed models are stable fixed points of the gradient flow, or ii) in sequential feature learning, where smaller modes take progressively longer to be learned, producing an effective collapse for a fixed training budget. Together these findings point to a trade-off between feature learning and collapse, suggesting an operator view as a step towards a unified framework for understanding the learning dynamics of dynamical systems-based generative models.

items.summary: The paper develops a learning theory for generative models based on dynamical systems, from normalizing flows to diffusion, using operator theory to analyze the gradient flow of a general class of stochastic differential equations. It explains the tension between feature learning and mode collapse empirically observed in continuous-time generative models.
items.reasoning: Theory explaining mode collapse in diffusion-type generative models addresses a widely felt gap; the use of dynamical systems and operator theory tools is rigorous and relevant to a large audience, though it is an early-step theoretical account rather than an immediately actionable result.

items.title: All roads lead to Markov kernel networks: A representation theorem for discretization-stable learning
items.content: arXiv:2611.10051v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Operator learning seeks to approximate function-to-function maps in a way that remains stable when the input discretization changes, a property sometimes called "discretization invariance". We consider a quantitative refinement of this idea, called $\textit{uniform discretization stability}$, which builds on a common representation of input functions and their discretizations as probability measures and provides a H\"older bound relating output changes to the Wasserstein distance between these measures. Our main result is a representation theorem showing all uniformly discretization stable operators can be written exactly as a $\textit{stable Markov kernel network}$---an abstract architecture that is a joint generalization of transformers, Fourier neural operators (FNO), Flowers, and other successful learned operators. Our representation theorem characterizes a design space for discretization-stable operator learning; designing new architectures becomes a question of which parts of a Markov kernel network to parameterize, and how. We further show that the read kernels of these networks can be realized as solutions of regularized variational problems, with particular choices of costs and regularizers recovering the kernels of transformers, FNO, Flowers, their hybrids, and beyond. This variational formulation provides a systematic approach to architecture design, together with sufficient conditions for uniform discretization stability.

Its practical impact is indirect but it provides principled grounding for a widely used assumption.

items.title: On the universal structure in deterministic generative diffusion
items.content: arXiv:2611.10338v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Diffusion-based generative modeling has emerged as a general computational framework for simulating high-dimensional, structured data across various domains. Understanding its generative mechanisms is paramount for advancing model training and inference in a principled way. Here, we demonstrate that deterministic sampling trajectories share a universal geometric structure invariant to data modalities and diffusion model implementations. This structure can be largely explained by an exactly solvable model based on the optimal linear denoiser.

items.title: Robust and Efficient Continual Model Merging via Global Singular Subspace Separation and Restoration
items.content: arXiv:2611.10881v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Continual model merging incrementally integrates task-specific models without revisiting past models or data. However, repeated merging entangles past task components and distorts their singular geometry, making balanced task-wise allocation increasingly difficult. We propose Global Singular Subspace Separation and Restoration (GS3R), which augments the merged update with a compact restoration state. At each merge, GS3R restores the retained singular geometry, separates task-wise subspaces, and globally reallocates the available rank across tasks fairly. To reduce merging-time memory overhead, we further introduce Pre-merge Restoration and Flushing (PRF). Experiments on vision, NLP, and multimodal benchmarks show that GS3R provides a strong accuracy-efficiency trade-off.

items.title: Uncertainty-Guided Reward Labeling for Reinforcement Learning under Limited Feedback
items.content: arXiv:2611.11091v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In reinforcement learning from limited feedback (RLLF), only a small fraction of an offline dataset can be labeled with rewards, and the central question is which samples should be labeled to learn a high-performing policy from the resulting partially labeled dataset. Prior work formalized this as a reward-selection problem by focusing on the selection stage while treating downstream policy learning as a black box, in a regime where queried rewards are not retained for reward-model training. We instead study the retained-label setting, where queried rewards can be stored and used to fit a reward model before policy learning. We bound the suboptimality of the learned policy in terms of two sources of error: one arising from offline RL on a fixed, offline dataset, and the other from uncertainty in the reward model. Since reward selection cannot change the offline dataset, the limited labeling budget must be used to strategically reduce reward uncertainty. Motivated by RLLF's observation that useful rewards tend to keep the agent on high-return trajectories, we introduce Successor-Guided Uncertainty REduction (SURE), a novel method that uses successor features to select rewards that are both uncertain and associated with states from which high-valued states are reachable. We formally derive SURE from a bound-induced design objective and characterize its exact one-step marginal gain. Empirically, SURE reaches near full-feedback performance with few reward labels across a variety of domains and offline-RL backbones, yielding an effective method for feedback-efficient reinforcement learning.

items.title: Compositional Conformal Risk Control for Multi-Stage LLM Cascades
items.content: arXiv:2611.11114v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Multi-stage large language model (LLM) cascades balance accuracy and inference cost, but reliable deployment also requires controlling error risk and identifying its sources across stages. We propose Compositional Conformal Risk Control (CompCRC), a risk-control framework for pre-specified multi-stage LLM cascades. We decompose the risk of accepting incorrect answers into additive stage-wise contributions over the full query population, linking local risk budgets to a system-level guarantee. CompCRC constructs and freezes candidate budget allocations and acceptance thresholds, selects one candidate on independent data, and certifies its stage-wise risk contributions on separate held-out data. Under conditional exchangeability, we establish a finite-sample guarantee: the marginal expected accepted-error risk of the complete deployment procedure does not exceed the global risk budget. At the reported comparison budget of $\alpha=0.45$, all three stages of CompCRC pass their local checks on MMLU, GSM8K, and HellaSwag. Compared with Global-CRC, which passes system-level risk certification at the same budget, CompCRC reduces observed accepted-error risk by 1.33--2.00 percentage points, improves final accuracy by 0.67--2.00 percentage points, and reduces weighted inference cost by 30.37\% on HellaSwag. The selected cost-based budget allocation also improves accuracy per unit cost by 10.6\%--46.7\% over uniform allocation. Further experiments show that stage-wise statistics identify stages that fail local certification checks, providing diagnostic information alongside system-level risk control.

items.title: Spatial Harness: Grounding Spatial Reasoning in Executable World States with Physics Engines
items.content: arXiv:2611.11344v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Spatial reasoning requires understanding how objects and observers are arranged in a scene and how their relations change with viewpoint or movement. Vision-language models (VLMs) typically perform both steps through model-internal reasoning, forming an implicit scene interpretation from partial views and imagining the consequences of spatial transformations. A misread scene can lead to a wrong answer, while even a correct interpretation does not ensure that imagined transformations satisfy spatial constraints. We introduce Spatial Harness, which represents scenes as explicit and executable world states to ground spatial reasoning in physics-engine feedback. A Perceiver integrates scene constraints extracted from the question with specialized visual estimates to place objects and cameras in a shared coordinate frame. The resulting state is instantiated in a physics engine, where a Reasoner executes viewpoint changes and uses computed measurements and rendered views to guide reasoning. We evaluate on MindCube, SAT, MMSI-Bench, and SpatialRGPT-Bench with open- and closed-weight VLMs. On MindCube, Spatial Harness improves Qwen3.5-27B from 52.70% to 71.14%, surpassing pySpatial by 7.52 percentage points. Given identical annotated object and camera poses, it reaches 98.25% versus 71.81% for model-internal reasoning. Code is publicly available at: https://github.com/tmlr-group/Spatial-Harness
items.author: Chentao Cao, Zhanke Zhou, Sangni Duan, Bo Han, Hang Li
items.summary: Spatial Harness improves VLM spatial reasoning by representing scenes as explicit, executable world states verified by physics-engine feedback rather than relying on implicit internal scene interpretation. A Perceiver integrates scene constraints from the question with specialized components to ground spatial transformations in simulation. This addresses a known VLM weakness: misread scenes and physically invalid imagined transformations.
items.reasoning: Well-motivated neuro-symbolic approach to a recognized VLM deficiency, with the appealing idea of executable world states as ground truth. Impact depends on benchmark results, but the direction is important for embodied and spatial reasoning.

items.title: A Trust Region Approach for Learning Schr\"{o}dinger Bridges
items.content: arXiv:2611.11649v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We study the numerical approximation of Schr\"{o}dinger Bridges in the setting where samples from the target distribution are unavailable and only an unnormalized target density is given. In this regime, the widely used iterative proportional fitting (IPF) procedure (and its variants) often exhibits severe numerical instabilities, stemming from ill-conditioned underlying control problems and from the fact that the optimal solution may lie far from the initialization. To address these issues, we propose a trust region variant of IPF that constrains successive updates to remain at a fixed Kullback-Leibler divergence from the current iterate. This restriction significantly improves numerical stability. Moreover, we show that the resulting method admits an interpretation as a mirror descent scheme with an adaptively chosen step size. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several challenging sampling tasks.

items.title: MOOD: Benchmarking Post-Hoc OOD Detection for Materials Property Prediction
items.content: arXiv:2611.11839v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection is essential for deploying machine learning models in high stakes scientific applications, yet methods that flag OOD inputs without retraining the model have been validated almost exclusively on image classification. We introduce MOOD (Materials Out-of-Distribution Detection), a benchmark for evaluating whether these post-hoc OOD detectors transfer to graph neural networks (GNNs) on materials property prediction. MOOD evaluates 15 post-hoc detectors and 2 supervised diagnostic probes across 4 GNN architectures, 5 MatBench tasks, and 15 physically motivated compositional and structural shifts, yielding 264 evaluation settings and over 13,000 AUROC measurements across three encoder training seeds. Our evaluation reveals three key findings. First, current post-hoc detectors perform near chance; all 15 detectors achieve an AUROC around 0.5. Second, detector failures decompose into two regimes: method bottlenecks and encoder bottlenecks. Method bottlenecks arise when supervised probes can separate in-distribution (ID) from OOD samples but unsupervised detectors fail, meaning that the embeddings contain OOD signal that current detectors do not extract. Encoder bottlenecks arise when even supervised probes fail to separate ID from OOD samples, indicating that the relevant shift is not accessible in the frozen GNN representation. Third, when OOD prediction error exceeds ID error, the AUROC of distance-based and density-based detectors correlates with the size of that gap. Collectively, these findings indicate that reliable OOD detection in scientific domains requires representation learning strategies that explicitly preserve OOD relevant signal, particularly for tasks where current GNN architectures encode no extractable signal at all.

items.title: HyInv Technical Report
items.content: arXiv:2611.11997v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Inverse folding designs amino-acid sequences for a given protein backbone, and screening needs many candidates that are both diverse and well folded. We present HyInv, a 1.96-million-parameter backbone-conditioned graph network with an encoder-decoder architecture, trained by Hyra 2.0, the research agent developed by our team: pretrained with random-order autoregressive sequence modeling, followed by structure-reward reinforcement learning. At inference, a grouped draft-and-rewrite sampler that uses separate draft and rewrite temperatures improves refolding TM-score at matched diversity. An optimized implementation with BF16 numerics designs 128 sequences for a 402-residue backbone in 50.6 ms on a single NVIDIA H20 GPU, about 52 times faster than the reference sampler, and an exact FP32 path that returns the reference sequences is 8.7 times faster. Across five benchmark datasets and seven dataset-predictor combinations, HyInv reaches a higher average scTM than all ten external baselines at comparable or higher sequence diversity, with large margins over ProteinMPNN and ProteinZero V2. The same default setting supports de novo backbones, pocket-constrained libraries, enzyme redesign with the catalytic site kept, and loop redesign. We have released our code and model at https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hyra-results/tree/main/AI4Science/hyinv.

items.title: XposedMIA: Exploiting Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) for One-Shot Membership Inference Attacks
items.content: arXiv:2611.12067v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Machine learning (ML) services increasingly expose explainability outputs alongside model predictions. While such explanations are intended to improve transparency, they may also reveal information about the underlying training data. In this work, we show that the local surrogate geometry employed by Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME) can be repurposed as a proxy for a sample's distance to the model's decision boundary. We extend this boundary-distance view to tabular counterfactual explanations and, for the first time, to visual counterfactual explanations for image classifiers. We present XposedMIA, a one-shot, explanation-based black-box membership inference attack (MIA) framework that converts the returned explanation into a proxy for the queried sample's distance to the model decision boundary. After a one-time calibration step on a small labeled calibration set of as few as 30 samples, our attack requires only a single query for each target sample. Unlike prior label-only attacks requiring iterative queries or shadow training, our method relies solely on the predicted label and its accompanying explanation. Our evaluation indicates that XposedMIA achieves high effectiveness, with success rates of up to 0.95 using only a single query per target, revealing that releasing explanations introduces an additional channel for membership leakage.
items.author: Omar Hamdache, Serdar Kara, K{\i}van\c{c} Kuzey Dikici, Abdullah \c{C}a\u{g}lar \"Oks\"uz, Anisa Halimi, Erman Ayday, Sinem Sav
items.summary: XposedMIA shows that explainability outputs (LIME's surrogate geometry, tabular counterfactuals, and visual counterfactuals for image classifiers) can be repurposed as proxies for a sample's distance to the model's decision boundary, enabling a one-shot black-box membership inference attack. It demonstrates that explainability features can leak training data membership.
items.reasoning: A significant privacy finding: the transparency mechanisms that ML services increasingly expose are themselves privacy attack surfaces. The extension to visual counterfactual explanations is novel, and the one-shot, black-box nature makes the attack practical. Well-scoped security research.

We extend this boundary-distance view to tabular counterfactual explanations and, for the first time, to visual counterfactual explanations for image classifiers. We present XposedMIA, a one-shot, explanation-based black-box membership inference attack (MIA) framework that converts the returned explanation into a proxy for the queried sample's distance to the model decision boundary. After a one-time calibration step on a small labeled calibration set of as few as 30 samples, our attack requires only a single query for each target sample. Unlike prior label-only attacks requiring iterative queries or shadow training, our method relies solely on the predicted label and its accompanying explanation. Our evaluation indicates that XposedMIA achieves high effectiveness, with success rates of up to 0.95 using only a single query per target, revealing that releasing explanations introduces an additional channel for membership leakage.

items.title: The Optimal Rate Constant of Heavy-Ball Momentum on Smooth Strongly Convex Functions
items.content: arXiv:2611.12310v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The heavy-ball method with a constant step size and a constant momentum parameter accelerates gradient descent on quadratics, but no choice of the two parameters does so on the class of smooth strongly convex functions. We determine how much faster than gradient descent it can be made on this class. Writing the best worst-case rate over all tunings as $1-c(\kappa)/\kappa$, where $\kappa$ is the condition number, we prove that $c(\kappa)$ tends to $8$ in every dimension of two or more. The lower bound on the rate holds for every tuning, because a tuning that is faster than $1-8/\kappa$ on quadratics follows a slowly decaying spiral on some function of two variables. The matching upper bound comes from an explicit tuning, with nearly the momentum of Polyak's tuning and a step size about $\sqrt{\kappa}/8$ times smaller, and from a Lyapunov function whose positivity is verified in exact arithmetic. Optimally tuned heavy-ball is therefore asymptotically four times faster than gradient descent on this class.

items.title: K-prop: Deep Online Learning by Backpropagating Temporal Kernels
items.content: arXiv:2611.12530v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Self-recurrence represents an important component for temporal processing in neural networks, both artificial and biological, where it appears naturally in the form of leaky integration. However, due to the complex temporal dependencies of the gradient, an efficient and effective method of online training is still lacking. Here we propose K-prop, a novel online learning method for leaky neural networks. It dramatically reduces the computational and memory cost of real time recurrent learning (RTRL) by propagating kernel gains. K-prop also outperforms existing RTRL approximations and achieves performance comparable to backpropagation through time in sequence learning, classification, and reinforcement learning tasks. We further analyze how its sole approximation affects gradient quality and identify conditions under which K-prop remains accurate and effective.

items.title: CoilStellaration: A Dataset and Benchmark for Engineering-Aware Stellarator Coilset Generation
items.content: arXiv:2611.12689v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Stellarators are fusion devices that use externally generated, three-dimensional magnetic fields to confine hot plasma and offer a promising route to commercial fusion. Their electromagnetic coils pose a challenging design problem: they must reproduce the target magnetic field while satisfying engineering constraints and remaining practical and cost-effective to manufacture. Finding suitable geometries is a highly nonlinear inverse problem that generally has neither a closed-form nor a unique solution. This problem lies at the heart of stellarator design. We introduce CoilStellaration, a dataset and benchmark for learning the mapping between coil geometries from target plasma magnetic fields and engineering requirements. The dataset contains 177,000 optimized filamentary coilsets targeting plasma equilibria from ConStellaration, with sampled engineering requirements and achieved geometric and magnetic-field metrics. It spans multiple coil counts and field-period numbers, supporting studies of both specialized and shared models across configurations. The benchmark asks models to predict coils conditioned on a target equilibrium and requirements on coil-coil and coil-plasma spacing, curvature, and magnetic-field error. We show that magnetic-field accuracy remains the main challenge, with learned models rarely satisfying all requirements simultaneously. However, using learned predictions to initialize conventional coil optimization can accelerate early progress. We release baseline models and evaluation code to support reproducible research on both direct coil generation and learned optimization initializations. By lowering the barrier for machine learning and optimization researchers to engage with stellarator coil design, we aim to accelerate progress toward practical, cost-effective stellarator power plants.
