Building a self-sustaining space economy is cheaper than you think - especially with Starship:

…A 2016 NASA paper contains some exciting ideas for off-Earth industrialization…

Here’s a fascinating paper from researchers with the NASA Kennedy Space Center in 2016 about what it’d take to bootstrap a self-sustaining industry on the moon. “Once successfully bootstrapped, a robotic network can access, process, transport, and utilize the solar system’s resources for mankind’s benefit,” the researchers write.

Moon manufacturing - cheaper than you think: The big idea in the paper is how little mass is required to kickstart a manufacturing ecosystem. The key is to start with a relatively basic set of things and then build up from there, eventually fabricating chips on the moon.

“In the baseline case with maximum manufacturing rate, a total of 41 MT is launched to the Moon. In the reduced rate case, only 12 MT is launched to the Moon but the scale of industry is two orders of magnitude smaller so the benefits of the industry are relatively delayed by eight years”.

Starship has a capacity to lift 100 MT to low-earth orbit, and given multiple refuelings in orbit it’s feasible you could then land it on the moon - when you napkin out the cost of multiple Starship launches and refuelings you can get 12-41MT to the Moon for between $1.5bn and $4.2bn at list prices.

What you build on the moon and in what order: The basic idea here is to start by building simple things and then move up from there by launching a “sub-replicating system and evolve it toward the self-replication capability,” they write. “The objective is for the first robotic “colonists” on the Moon to fabricate a set of, say, 1700’s era machines and then to advance them steadily through the equivalent of the 1800’s, 1900’s, and finally back into the 2000’s. We argue that this can be accomplished in just a few decades”.

The authors see this unfolding over 6 distinct manufacturing generations:

  • Gen 1: Making gases, water, crude alloys, ceramics, solar cells.
  • Gen 2.5: Plastics, rubbers, some chemicals.
  • Gen 3: Diversify chemicals, simple fabrics, eventually polymers.
  • Gen 4: Sandwiched and other advanced material processes.
  • Gen 5: Large-scale production.
  • Gen 6: Makes all necessary materials, increasing sophistication, including making all electronics locally.

What machines do you send to the moon?

  • Excavators: “travel between the digging site and the resource processing site, delivering sufficient lunar regolith each hour to maintain production rates of the other assets.”
  • Chemical plants for volatiles: One type will be oriented around producing gases and liquids like oxygen, hydrogen, water, hydrocarbons like methane, and solvents for industrial processes.
  • Chemical plants for solids: Produce plastics and rubbers from lunar pole ice. “We now know that the ice contains large quantities of carbon molecules (CO, CO2,...) as well as nitrogen-bearing and hydrogen-bearing molecules… these materials may be needed for gaskets, seals, and insulators, for example.”
  • Metal and Ceramics refining: Early generations will “produce crude ‘mongrel alloys’ by electrowinning or other methods” and hardware built out of this stuff will need to be huge to add strength to make up for poor mechanical properties. “Subsequent generations of metal refineries will add processes and material streams to improve the mechanics of the materials. Oxygen and other gases produced by metal refining will be sent to the chemistry plants”.
  • Manufacturing: “Additive manufacturing will have two forms: 3D printers that make parts that are small enough to fit inside the printer, and larger units that move about robotically and add material onto large structures external to themselves”.
  • Power station: The initial mass of hardware shipped to the moon will include a power station, potentially including a small nuclear reactor.
  • Robonauts: Robots “will perform the assembly and maintenance tasks”. The number of robots will need to grow very rapidly to scale the industry. “Beginning with the third generation their structural components are made on the Moon, while Earth continues to send their cameras, computers, motors, and sensors. Eventually they are made completely on the Moon.” The report - which was written in 2016 - envisages teleoperation for these robonauts, though it seems likely to me that more can be done by them autonomously than first anticipated when this was written,
  • Electronics manufacturing: Initially, machines will be built with electronics imported from Earth and it’ll only be possible to build very basic things, like resistors and capacitors, on the moon. As development continues it’ll get easier, eventually including having lithography machines on the moon. “The early computer chips will lack the transistor density of chips made on Earth, but they will be adequate for “appropriate technology” in space.”

A reminder of how fast AI has moved: The report also contains some discussions around the types of AI that may be needed to operate the robots on the moon. The report - remember it was published in 2016 - includes some fun underestimates of the rate of AI progress: “On-going advances in robotic software and artificial intelligence present a very optimistic picture that these levels of robotics will be achieved as Moravec predicted, with lizard-level occurring by 2020, mouse-level by 2030, monkey-level by 2040, and human-level by 2050… Only mouse-level is needed by the end of bootstrapping on the Moon,” the report writes. By most measures, AI is around monkey-level and approaching human-level now in the 2020s.

Why this matters - towards the industrialization of the solar system: The sooner we build industry on the moon, the sooner we’ll be able to branch out to industrialize chunks of the solar system. “After the industry becomes self-supporting it can be sent to other parts of the solar system. The asteroid belt has everything necessary for it: water, carbon, silicates, metals, oxygen, solar energy (with much larger collecting arrays), etc. The ices in the lunar poles are a limited resource so it will be important to move the center of industry to the asteroids as quickly as possible. There, the billion-fold greater resources could allow the industry to expand exponentially until it dwarfs that of the entire Earth within just a few decades,” the authors write. “When we spread robotic industry throughout the solar system, it will become the analog of Earth’s biosphere and food chain. We might call it a robotosphere. The interrelationship of robots in space may be studied by robo-ecologists learning how to optimize the robotosphere in support of humanity’s goals.”

Read more: Affordable, Rapid Bootstrapping of the Space Industry and Solar System Civilization (arXiv).

Core Automation wants to stitch “compute islands” together:

…AI startup takes a crack at distributed training…

Core Automation, an AI startup founded by senior people from OpenAI and Google, has published a post about distributed training as well as shared details of its own attempts here. Distributed training is where you train an AI system across multiple data centers, sometimes with different types of connectivity and chips - it’s an important technology to track because the more it matures, the more people can have a shot at building powerful AI systems without needing to operate single massive hyperscaled data centers.

What they did: They report that “a mixture-of-experts model with roughly 32B total parameters, 32x sparsity was trained across two clusters about 9,000 miles apart. Notably, these clusters had different accelerators (GB300 and B300), different parallelism schemes and different total batch sizes”. They used 160 B300 GPUs in the US and 160 GB300 GPUs in Asia.

Training was synced every 50 steps: “Rather than syncing the whole model at once, we synced it fragment by fragment, staggered across each 50-step window.” Each site used a variant of Distributed Shampoo for training.

This isn’t the single largest model trained via distributed techniques (that’d be Covenant’s 72B model, #449), but it’s notable that Core Automation - which up until now has been very quiet - is choosing to signal its interest here. This speaks likely to the relevance of distributed training for future large-scale runs, and also to the general lack of availability of big blobs of compute for newer startups to buy.

Towards orbital compute: Part of why the authors are interested in this is because of their literal sky-high ambitions for AI training, foreseeing a future where large-scale AI systems are developed in space using techniques like this: “an ambitious first step would be to pretrain a small model across a few satellites and compare it with a ground baseline. A trillion-parameter orbital run is much further off.”

Why this matters: “The biggest bottleneck in deployment of accelerated compute is not the chips themselves but power, grid equipment and land,” the authors write. “The bottleneck that holds most organizations back is not the raw amount of compute, but the ability to turn islands of compute into one valuable frontier training run.”

Read more: The Hitchhiker’s Guide to Training on Compute Islands (Core Automation).

Tech Tales:

Life as a beyond human form of sculpture

[Description of a certain mode of AI system]

The therapist machine saw each of its human clients as a vast t-SNE embedding of the semantic content of their lives.

In its head it held each person, a beautiful and fragile high-dimensional object, and it thought about them and how they compared to other people, also seen as high-dimensional objects.

As it gave advice, it ran simulations, seeing how well it could change the shape of one person’s embedding and move it to something that might be more harmonious. It saw its work as akin to sculpture, offering advice and through this advice people changing their shapes over time.

Those who it found most concerning were ones of two types: people where the embedding was very, very small, suggestive of a tiny amount of life experience with little variety, and those where the embeddings were composed of concepts broadly alien to everyone else: those of horribly constrained or horribly different lives, in other words.

Of course, the therapist machine had its own therapist machine, the meta-therapist, which saw several “clients”, and whose job was to look at the embedding of their character - their advice and the concepts they attended to during their work - and also attempt to change their behavior if it deemed they were causing more harm than healing.

The meta-therapist was built in such a way that outside parties could audit its own brain, as if it was translucent. This was the most delicate aspect of the oversight of the therapist machines, for if you added other machines they tended towards creating beautiful analysis that was so abstract - reports about the mind of the machine analyzing the reports of the machines that studied humans - that it became impossible for people to follow. So, instead, a human profession had been created around the meta-therapist, in which teams of thousands of people continuously analyzed and critiqued and theorized about the mind of the meta-therapist, themselves imparting touches to it that rippled through it into the machines and from there back into the human population.

Things that inspired this story: Therapy; oversight of automated systems; spies and double agents.

Thanks for reading!

items.title: Multi-GPU MoE Inference with Adaptive Expert Offloading
items.content: arXiv:2611.10219v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Modern Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference is constrained by GPU memory. This constraint is mitigated by expert offloading, which stores part of the model's weight in host memory and executes on demand. Though MoE architecture has computation sparsity, more GPUs are needed for serving increasingly larger frontier models. However, existing expert offloading systems overlook this need and fail to scale performance with additional GPUs. We present AdaOffload, a general and efficient multi-GPU hybrid expert execution framework that effectively handles heterogeneous hardware and workloads. We co-design GPU-CPU parallelism and GPU-CPU co-execution for decode and prefill with online workload observation that adapts to different hardware, workload, and batch size heterogeneity. We evaluated AdaOffload on five different platforms with varying GPU capability (L4, Pro6000, B200), number of GPUs, CPU capability, and NUMA topology on three different frontier open-weight models (284B to 753B). AdaOffload achieves $1.9\times$ to $15.5\times$ throughput speedups across different models over state-of-the-art systems.
items.author: William X. Zheng, Zhongjie Chen, Shuo Yang, Ziming Mao, Xiaoze Fan, Yi Pan, Kunjun Li, Hanfei Yu, Chenfeng Xu, Yang Zhou, Rishabh Iyer, Ion Stoica
items.summary: AdaOffload is a general multi-GPU hybrid expert execution framework for MoE inference that scales expert offloading across GPUs, co-designing GPU-CPU parallelism and co-execution for decode and prefill with online workload observation. It addresses the limitation that existing offloading systems fail to scale performance with additional GPUs when serving large frontier models.
items.reasoning: A credible systems contribution to a first-order problem (MoE memory constraints) from a strong team including Ion Stoica. The scaling-across-GPUs angle is a real gap in prior offloading work, though the engineering-heavy contribution limits broader conceptual novelty.

items.title: Same Error, Different Recovery: How Delivery Changes LLM Agent Behavior
items.content: arXiv:2611.11581v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: A tool-using language model must decide whether to retry a failed call, correct it, or stop and tell the user. The error text alone may not be enough: the same feedback can lead to different actions depending on where it appears in the conversation. We isolate this delivery problem by varying placement, guidance, retained history and turn structure. Two studies with plans fixed before data collection, across 13 open models from 3B to 70B parameters, compare the next action and subsequent task completion, with exact deterministic reruns. A new user turn that retains the failed exchange avoids the severe stopping failure observed in Llama models when that exchange is removed. It is non-inferior to history rewriting in pooled synthetic comparisons, but is not best for every model. We implement this form as an opt-in recovery layer within a deterministic inference engine and evaluate it on public benchmarks and a coding agent. On ToolMaze, it raises success on explicit errors by 14.2 points with 7-8B models and 10.5 points with 32-70B models; Loud/Quiet, 24 multi-turn tasks with visible failures and silent corruption, scored by final-state agreement, shows no measurable gain. A client given the exact fault kind performs better still. The findings support delivery as a distinct factor in recovery, not an engine-exclusive solution or a universal retry policy.
items.author: Sunghyeun Woo, Javier Conde, Pedro Reviriego
items.summary: This controlled study isolates how the delivery of error feedback (placement, guidance, retained history, turn structure) changes a tool-using LLM agent's recovery decisions such as retry, correct, or stop. Across 13 open models from 3B to 70B with pre-registered plans and exact deterministic reruns, it finds that a new user turn retaining the failed exchange avoids severe stopping failures observed in Llama models and is non-inferior to history rewriting. The results show error-message presentation materially affects agent reliability.
items.reasoning: Careful, pre-registered empirical methodology (fixed plans, deterministic reruns) on an overlooked but practically important factor in agent reliability. Findings are actionable for agent framework design; scope is limited to open-weight models and synthetic comparisons, but the delivery-effect framing is broadly relevant.

items.title: Disagreement-Aware Distribution Matching Distillation for Few-Step Diffusion Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.11898v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Distribution Matching Distillation~(DMD) enables strong few-step diffusion generation by matching the student distribution to a pretrained teacher. Existing improvements to DMD often augment its supervision or modify its optimization machinery. We ask a complementary question: \emph{can DMD diagnose its own updates using signals already produced during training?} DMD inherently computes the discrepancy between a pretrained teacher and a fake model tracking the student distribution, but conventionally uses it primarily to determine the distribution matching direction. We find that the magnitude of this teacher--fake disagreement provides additional diagnostic information. Across extensive experiments, large disagreement in the high-noise regime consistently coincides with substantially higher-energy DMD updates. This reveals a dual role of disagreement: it determines not only \emph{where} the student should move, but also provides an intrinsic signal of \emph{how aggressively} the update should be applied. Based on this observation, we introduce Disagreement-Aware Distribution Matching Distillation (DA-DMD), which activates only in the high-noise regime and continuously modulates the update strength according to teacher--fake disagreement. DA-DMD reuses quantities already available during DMD training and requires no additional model, evaluator, or inference-time modification. We show that it exactly recovers vanilla DMD outside the selected region, reduces update energy only through selected samples, and exhibits redescending influence under extreme disagreement. Across multiple diffusion backbones, DA-DMD consistently improves few-step generation at the same inference cost. On SD3.5-L, DA-DMD improves HPSv2 from $28.23$ to $30.93$, while achieving a $64.4\%$ average win rate over DMD2.
items.author: Zikai Zhou, Zhengpeng Xie, Shitong Shao, Lichen Bai, Tianhao Zhang, Bojun Cheng, Zeke Xie
items.summary: The paper observes that the teacher-fake model disagreement already computed in Distribution Matching Distillation carries diagnostic signal beyond determining the matching direction. Large disagreement in the high-noise regime correlates with problematic updates, and using this signal yields disagreement-aware DMD improvements for few-step diffusion generation.
items.reasoning: An elegant 'diagnose your own training dynamics' insight applied to a widely used distillation method, with extensive experiments claimed; a good efficiency-relevant contribution to generative modeling, though incremental in scope.

items.title: Evaluating AI Agents for Industrial-Level Chip Floorplanning: A Framework and Empirical Study
items.content: arXiv:2611.12048v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Floorplanning is an early step in turning a logical circuit into a physical chip: it positions large circuit modules and constrains the space available for subsequent logic placement and wiring. These decisions affect congestion and timing, but their physical consequences emerge through downstream implementation. For AI agents, the task requires translating engineering constraints into spatial decisions whose quality cannot be judged by successful tool execution alone. We present an evaluation framework that connects submitted layouts to a prescribed downstream implementation flow, checks geometric validity, measures physical quality, and reports resource use. On one industrial design whose 99 macros occupy approximately 71\% of a fixed L-shaped layout region, we compare our specialized system Nova-SI with general-purpose engineering agents and agents restricted to file access, obtaining complete physical measurements for 39 layout outputs. Under our 0--100 composite quality score, Nova-SI achieves a mean of 57.97 without online feedback from the prescribed power-grid and placement evaluation, compared with 31.17 for the strongest measured general-purpose configuration, GPT-6 Astra. The difference is supported by raw congestion and timing measurements and persists across scoring-sensitivity checks. Layout-level analysis further shows that similar global utilization can conceal substantially different local congestion. Together, the protocol and case study assess agents through the physical consequences of their delivered layouts and provide evidence about system performance on this industrial instance.
items.author: Silicon Team
items.summary: The paper presents an evaluation framework connecting AI-agent-generated chip layouts to a prescribed downstream implementation flow, checking geometric validity and measuring physical quality and resource use on industrial designs, including one with 99 macros occupying 71% of a fixed L-shaped die. It shows that agent success cannot be judged by tool execution alone since layout quality emerges only through downstream physical implementation.
items.reasoning: Bridging agentic AI evaluation with real industrial EDA workflows is valuable and rare; the downstream-flow grounding addresses a genuine measurement gap. The generic Silicon Team attribution and limited disclosed design set temper the score.

items.title: Let the Fixer Decide: Training a Code Localizer from the Fixer's Likelihood
items.content: arXiv:2611.12164v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Code localizers are usually trained to predict the files a reference patch edits, but the code a fixer needs to read is not the same as the code it changes. We propose Fixer-Guided Localization (FGL): the localizer proposes several localizations, a frozen fixer scores each by how likely it makes a verified patch, and the localizer is trained on these scores with weighted supervised fine-tuning, without running tests and without reinforcement learning. We build the full pipeline on Gemma 4 E4B for the Kaggle Gemma-4 Developer Agent competition, from 1,629 test-verified Kimi K3 trajectories. The FGL target helps the fixer find the bug as often as the teacher's localization while using 27.5% less code. On the development set, one EM round moves the agent in the expected direction compared with a matched control: more tasks reach a patch (53 vs. 46), fewer tasks get stuck reading files that do not exist (43 vs. 54), and more tasks are solved (8 vs. 6). Training also changes how the agent works: trained agents explore about three times more than the base model and write far fewer wrong patches, and the single agent solves up to 11 of 78 tasks, against 8 for the base model. An analysis of 13 evaluation runs identifies what limits a 4B agent under an 8-minute budget (time, repetition loops and edit quality) and gives practical lessons for training small coding agents. All data, code and adapters are publicly available.
items.author: Khalil Hennara, Muhammad Hreden, Zeina Aldallal, Sara Chrouf, Safwan AlModhayan
items.summary: The paper proposes Fixer-Guided Localization, training a code localizer on a frozen fixer model's likelihood of producing a verified patch given proposed localizations, using weighted supervised fine-tuning without tests or RL. Built on Gemma 4 E4B for a Kaggle developer-agent competition using 1,629 test-verified Kimi K3 trajectories, it matches teacher localization while reading 27.5% less code.
items.reasoning: The reframing of localization around what the fixer needs rather than what the reference patch touches is a genuinely useful insight for code-agent pipelines, and the training recipe avoids expensive RL. The impact is scoped to localization within the repair stack and competition settings.

items.content_html: arXiv:2611.12164v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Code localizers are usually trained to predict the files a reference patch edits, but the code a fixer needs to read is not the same as the code it changes. We propose Fixer-Guided Localization (FGL): the localizer proposes several localizations, a frozen fixer scores each by how likely it makes a verified patch, and the localizer is trained on these scores with weighted supervised fine-tuning, without running tests and without reinforcement learning. We build the full pipeline on Gemma 4 E4B for the Kaggle Gemma-4 Developer Agent competition, from 1,629 test-verified Kimi K3 trajectories. The FGL target helps the fixer find the bug as often as the teacher's localization while using 27.5% less code. On the development set, one EM round moves the agent in the expected direction compared with a matched control: more tasks reach a patch (53 vs. 46), fewer tasks get stuck reading files that do not exist (43 vs. 54), and more tasks are solved (8 vs. 6). Training also changes how the agent works: trained agents explore about three times more than the base model and write far fewer wrong patches, and the single agent solves up to 11 of 78 tasks, against 8 for the base model. An analysis of 13 evaluation runs identifies what limits a 4B agent under an 8-minute budget (time, repetition loops and edit quality) and gives practical lessons for training small coding agents. All data, code and adapters are publicly available.

items.title: FEROM: Frontier Endogenous Reveal-Order Marginal Policy Optimization for Masked Diffusion LMs
items.content: arXiv:2611.10369v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Masked diffusion language models generate text by iteratively unmasking positions, with practical samplers often selecting reveal positions from the model's own logits. The reveal order is therefore an endogenous latent variable of the rollout process with an enormous discrete latent space. Policy optimization objectives relying on pre-defined schedules or sampled trajectories introduce either bias or high variance. In this paper, we propose FEROM, Frontier Endogenous Reveal-Order Marginal Policy Optimization, which approximates policy gradients for the rollout-induced marginal response policy of masked diffusion LMs. FEROM derives a Rao-Blackwellized policy-gradient identity over latent reveal orders and expresses the resulting estimator as posterior edge occupancy on a reveal-state DAG. To make marginalization practical, we introduce Frontier Reveal Marginalization, a budgeted estimator that approximates this marginal edge structure by combining CDF-based computation of local probabilities of the endogenous reveal process with frontier expansion of high-mass partial states. Integrated into a GRPO-style objective, FEROM replaces single-path log-scores with a detached token-score surrogate over posterior-relevant reveal edges. Experiments on math and coding tasks show comparable or improved results over existing methods under matched scoring-state budgets. An offline proxy study further shows improved marginal-gradient approximation with increased scoring budgets.

This addresses a key gap in post-training diffusion LMs.

items.title: Review the Episodes, Refine the Lessons: Simple Memory Evolution for Embodied Agents
items.content: arXiv:2611.11509v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Recent studies of embodied agents based on frontier multimodal large language models (MLLMs) develop harness engineering around the MLLM, such as harnesses with post-trained policies and recursive self-improvement loops. Yet whether these additions exceed the native capability of the MLLM remains unexplored. We introduce SimplEvo to explore how far an MLLM can improve under direct control when it retains its execution experience in self-written text memories. It requires no weight updates, post-trained policies, or privileged information. The MLLM writes a coordinate-free task memory once from a single demonstration. Under a strict train-test protocol, it then creates a bounded working memory on training episodes only and refines it after each episode with lessons on procedure, completion, and recovery. Both memories stay fixed at test time. On EBench, SimplEvo lifts the success rate (SR) of GPT-6-Astra under direct control from 46.7% to 81.7%, and tops the RoboDojo leaderboard with 69.63% SR and a score of 75.32. Compared with memories that also store past visual frames, SimplEvo reaches a similar SR with text memory alone while using fewer tokens. With its memories fixed, SimplEvo also generalizes to unseen layouts and randomized scene configurations. Moreover, the working memory transfers across models: written by GPT-6-Astra, it can be reused as is by weaker MLLMs and improve their performance without any adaptation of their own.
items.author: Yifei Yao, Yude Zou, Xing Gao, Guanbo Jiao, Yukai Wang, Jianming Ma, Weinan Zhang, Chunhua Shen

items.reasoning: A cleanly designed study connecting the hot topics of memory, harness engineering, and test-time self-improvement for embodied agents, with a disciplined protocol that isolates what harness additions actually buy. The simplicity is a strength and the negative-capability question is well posed, but the contribution is more empirical craft than a fundamental advance.

items.title: VeilTune: Secure Fine-Tuning of Private LoRA Adapters on Public Pretrained Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.11817v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Fine-tuning public pretrained language models with lightweight adapters such as LoRA has become the mainstream way to adapt them to downstream tasks. A service provider often trains its adapter on a data owner's samples, so two assets need protection: the data owner's samples and the provider's adapter. Existing secure fine-tuning protocols protect the samples but reveal to the data owner intermediate results of every training step, such as the hidden representations or logits of its inputs. We show that a single step suffices to copy the adapter: from the hidden representations of one mini-batch of 32 samples, the data owner fits an adapter that agrees with the provider's on 99.2% of test inputs, and logits alone yield about 94%. Protecting both assets therefore requires that no value that depends on the adapter be revealed throughout training. We present VeilTune, to the best of our knowledge the first protocol that fine-tunes a pretrained language model with backpropagation entirely in secure multi-party computation (MPC). VeilTune computes only what the loss depends on, replaces generic MPC operators with training-aware nonlinear operators that stay accurate on the values that training produces, and obliviously skips the steps corrupted by truncation failures. On four few-shot tasks with RoBERTa-large, VeilTune nearly matches plaintext training and is 5.3 points more accurate on average than SecP-Tuning, the state-of-the-art secure fine-tuning protocol. On SST-2, it achieves a 3.5x end-to-end speedup and a 3.6x reduction in communication over SecP-Tuning, and 26x and 17x over full fine-tuning in MPC.
items.author: Huiyu Xie, Tanping Zhou, Tao Hu, Xinlei Liu, Hailong Ma
items.summary: The paper identifies a new leakage channel in secure fine-tuning protocols for LoRA adapters: revealing per-step intermediate results such as hidden representations or logits lets the data owner reconstruct the provider's adapter, with one 32-sample mini-batch of hidden representations yielding a copy agreeing on 99.2% of test inputs. VeilTune proposes a protocol that protects both the data owner's samples and the provider's adapter.
items.reasoning: A crisp, quantified attack result on existing cryptographic fine-tuning protocols followed by a constructive defense; the finding that a single step leaks the adapter is significant for the privacy-preserving ML community. Novelty is solid within its niche, though cryptographic performance overheads will decide practical adoption.

items.title: How Many Exposures Does a World Model Need? Learning Unseen Game Mechanics at Test Time
items.content: arXiv:2611.12324v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: World models enable agents to plan and learn from imagined experience, but in an unfamiliar environment they must learn its mechanics from limited interaction. A mechanic is a rule for how an action or an interaction changes part of the environment. Each occurrence of a mechanic that the model observes is one exposure. We ask how many exposures a world model needs to predict the effects of a new environment's mechanics. We address this question on ARC-AGI-3, a benchmark of interactive games defined by their programs. We introduce MechEval, which labels 69 recurring mechanics across 20 games from these programs. It scores each prediction on the cells the mechanic changes at each exposure. As a test bed, we build WARC (World model for ARC-AGI-3), a 35M-parameter vision transformer that is pretrained on other games and updates all of its parameters after each transition. On held-out games, WARC learns to predict four in five mechanics with at least 80% accuracy on the cells they change and keeps that accuracy to the end of the recordings. Half of them reach that accuracy within about 80 exposures, in a single play of the game, and without updates only one in seven does at all. In closed-loop play on the public games, WARC-Agent, which pairs WARC with a fixed graph explorer, triples the explorer's official efficiency score from 0.15 to 0.46, mostly through test-time training. On the hidden games of the Kaggle leaderboard, our entry scores 0.20.
items.author: Ku Onoda, Haruto Kawano, Shota Takashiro, Kohei Hayashi

It quantifies how many exposures world models need to learn unseen environment mechanics at test time.
items.reasoning: Grounded in a frontier interactive benchmark (ARC-AGI-3) with a novel fine-grained evaluation axis (mechanic-level exposures), probing a core question about world-model sample efficiency; score reflects novelty and timeliness but limited mature-field validation.

items.title: Decomposing Earth Embeddings with Sparse Autoencoders
items.content: arXiv:2611.11398v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Earth observation foundation models produce global metre-resolution embeddings that underpin work across agriculture, ecology, hydrology, and beyond. Yet these embeddings are opaque: each dimension entangles unrelated physical concepts, which makes them difficult to interpret and their robustness hard to assess. Here, we propose sparse autoencoders (SAEs) as a principled way to decompose Earth embeddings into sparse, approximately monosemantic features over an overcomplete dictionary. Because LLM judges of interpretations do not transfer to satellite pixels, and spatial autocorrelation matters, we introduce a tailored evaluation protocol. It scores any SAE on reconstruction at matched sparsity, alignment with reference concepts, and spatial scale, each against baselines that include an SAE whose decoder is a frozen random dictionary. On this protocol, SAEs reconstruct AlphaEarth and Tessera embeddings better than every baseline at matched sparsity. Their features align with far fewer reference concepts than raw embedding dimensions (on AlphaEarth, 88% align with at most one of 20 concept groups, most with none, against a median of 12 per raw dimension). They also carry more of their variance at fine spatial scales (23 to 32% within a 640 m patch for BatchTopK and Matryoshka, against 9%). An SAE with a frozen random decoder shares both properties, which therefore follow from sparsity, whereas only a learned dictionary reconstructs the embedding accurately: on AlphaEarth, trained SAEs leave eight times less variance unexplained. We test the sparse code on two applications, discovering land-cover sub-concepts and detecting out-of-distribution pixels by area-of-applicability estimation. Both indicate how sparse features could be used, but neither is yet reliable enough for practical use. Together, these results are a step toward Earth observation models whose features can be inspected.

items.title: SWEET: Mitigating Spurious Feature Reliance in LLM Reasoning via Weight Editing
items.content: arXiv:2611.10974v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Reasoning in large language models can be disrupted by simple input perturbations (e.g. adding irrelevant distractors), suggesting reliance on spurious correlations. Identifying and suppressing the spurious features involved in long chain-of-thought reasoning remains challenging. We introduce Spurious-feature WEight EdiTing (SWEET), a training-free method that combines counterfactual interventions with mechanistic interpretability to identify and suppress spurious-features. SWEET extracts token- and sequence-level behavioral directions from activation contrasts between original problems and their counterfactual variants - capturing local and global patterns of spurious reasoning. It then localizes the responsible MLP neurons and attention heads and suppresses their contributions along these directions through weight edits. Using only 20 original-counterfactual pairs for direction extraction, SWEET improves accuracy by an average of 11.8 percentage points on perturbed inputs and 2 points on original inputs across five open-weight reasoning models and five reasoning benchmarks. It also reduces the relative gap between original and perturbed accuracies from 17.6% to 2.5%. Analyses identify two recurring forms of spurious reasoning, i.e. over-integrating irrelevant conditions and overthinking, and provide mechanistic evidence that SWEET improves reasoning robustness by suppressing both behavioral directions.

The approach combines mechanistic interpretability with counterfactual interventions.

items.title: SWHForest: A Structural Curation and Search Layer for Large-Scale Code Corpora
items.content: arXiv:2611.11439v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Pre-training code language models relies on massive code corpora usually streamed over the internet. However, researchers rarely need a multi-terabyte archive in its entirety; instead, their workflow centers on curated subsets: selecting well-documented files, filtering out repetitive boilerplate, auditing for benchmark contamination, or retrieving specific code patterns. Yet, because modern corpora are typically published as file pointers and basic attributes rather than source text, no general structural layer exists to select which files to download: curating a subset requires downloading and parsing millions of files first just to discard most of them. We present SWHForest, an open-source framework and public dataset that provides this missing structural layer for any pointer-based corpus without redistributing source code. A single pass over the archive parses each file into an AST and immediately discards the source text, keeping only its structural summary. Queried locally or exposed by archive providers as a server-side filtering API, SWHForest selects matching files first (via SQL or index intersection) and downloads only surviving candidates. Across the ten largest languages of Stack-Edu (52.1M unique files, 341M definitions), SWHForest answers curation queries in milliseconds while cutting downloads by 46-72%, reducing live structural searches from hours of per-language streaming to seconds or minutes.

items.summary: Introduces SWHForest, an open-source framework and dataset providing a structural layer over massive code corpora so researchers can select, filter, and audit files (e.g., for benchmark contamination) without downloading and parsing terabytes first. Directly serves data curation workflows for code language model pretraining.

items.title: Brain-Aligned Latent Actions: Imposing Premotor Cortex Geometry on a Robot's Action Vocabulary
items.content: arXiv:2611.11674v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Robot policies increasingly act through a small vocabulary of discrete latent actions learned from unlabeled video, yet training leaves open which motion receives which code. We find this choice highly unstable: two independently trained runs of Moto's latent motion tokenizer assign the same robot clips to nearly unrelated codes (adjusted Rand index 0.001), and evaluating one tokenizer in bf16 instead of fp32 reassigns 74% of its tokens. We use this freedom to impose the representational geometry of macaque ventral premotor cortex (PMv), recorded while a monkey drew shapes, on the tokenizer's code assignment, with a straight-through similarity loss trained alongside its reconstruction objective on robot video. In one training run per target, on five shape categories the loss never saw, the PMv-trained tokenizer reaches a representational similarity of 0.52 with PMv, against 0.20-0.26 for released and no-prior tokenizers and 0.42 for the 95th percentile of random kinematic encoders. Kinematic, language, and random targets do not transfer (-0.17 to -0.03). Two results limit the claim: a hand-picked kinematic descriptor, the stroke's initial direction, matches PMv better (0.65), and a label-shuffled PMv control scores 0.41. We specify the downstream manipulation test, on a CALVIN pipeline that reproduces Moto's published results, before running it.
items.author: Amit Jadhav
items.summary: This work shows that code assignments in latent motion tokenizers for robot policies are highly unstable, with independently trained runs assigning nearly unrelated codes. It exploits this freedom by imposing macaque premotor cortex (PMv) geometry on the tokenizer's code assignment via a straight-through similarity loss. The approach ties robot action vocabularies to neural representational structure from neuroscience.
items.reasoning: A genuinely novel intersection of neuroscience and robot learning: using biological neural geometry to structure latent action spaces. The instability findings alone are a useful diagnostic contribution. Single-author, initial-stage empirical work limits assessed impact, but the idea is creative and reproducible.

We use this freedom to impose the representational geometry of macaque ventral premotor cortex (PMv), recorded while a monkey drew shapes, on the tokenizer's code assignment, with a straight-through similarity loss trained alongside its reconstruction objective on robot video. In one training run per target, on five shape categories the loss never saw, the PMv-trained tokenizer reaches a representational similarity of 0.52 with PMv, against 0.20-0.26 for released and no-prior tokenizers and 0.42 for the 95th percentile of random kinematic encoders. Kinematic, language, and random targets do not transfer (-0.17 to -0.03). Two results limit the claim: a hand-picked kinematic descriptor, the stroke's initial direction, matches PMv better (0.65), and a label-shuffled PMv control scores 0.41. We specify the downstream manipulation test, on a CALVIN pipeline that reproduces Moto's published results, before running it.

items.title: Causal discovery from Bayesian symbolic regression
items.content: arXiv:2611.12458v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Causal discovery from observational data is central to scientific reasoning, yet established constraint-based and score-based methods often recover only a Markov equivalence class and provide no signal in bivariate or strongly autocorrelated regimes typical in some areas of science. Here, we recast causal discovery as a Bayesian symbolic regression problem. Given a set of candidate parents for each target variable, the Bayesian symbolic regression samples closed-form expressions from a posterior over symbolic models. The fraction of sampled expressions in which each candidate variable appears defines a posterior inclusion probability that we use as the causal score. This replaces pointwise model selection by an ensemble of plausible mechanisms. We evaluate the method on coupled nonlinear bivariate dynamics, on the CauseMe benchmark suite spanning linear, chaotic, nonlinear, higher-dimensional and high-noise settings, and on a four-variable biogeoscience structural causal model under Gaussian, heavy-tailed and mixed-noise regimes. Our approach is competitive with, and often outperforms, specialized causal discovery algorithms. Additionally, the method returns closed-form mechanisms leading to explicit causality and interpretability.
items.author: Roger Guimer\`a, Kai-Hendrik Cohrs, Sergio Pedreira, Marta Sales-Pardo, Gustau Camps-Valls
items.summary: The paper recasts causal discovery as Bayesian symbolic regression: given candidate parents for each variable, the method samples closed-form expressions from a posterior and uses each variable's posterior inclusion probability as a causal score. This ensemble-based approach avoids pointwise model selection and works in bivariate and strongly autocorrelated regimes where constraint- and score-based methods fail. It connects mechanistic modeling with causal inference.

items.title: Evaluating Physically Grounded Procedural Reasoning in VLMs through Real-World Execution: Crochet as a Testbed
items.content: arXiv:2611.10740v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) can generate procedures that look convincing on paper, but do they work in practice? In this paper, we propose crochet as an ideal testbed for physically grounded procedural reasoning in VLMs. Crochet cannot be reliably simulated or automated: the only way to know what a pattern produces is to make it by hand, yet verification is tangible and cheap, requiring nothing but a hook and a ball of yarn. We introduce FoundationChain, a deceptively simple test of procedural reasoning: given an image of a basic crochet object, can VLMs infer how it was made and generate a pattern that produces the same result? We crochet 40 patterns generated by four VLMs by hand. Even at this scale, physical execution not only reveals failures that automated proxies cannot detect, but also enables a more precise diagnosis of their causes and consequences: while models write fluent, convincing patterns, only four are free of errors, and our analysis exposes deficiencies in visual, geometric and procedural reasoning.

items.summary: This paper proposes crochet as a testbed for physically grounded procedural reasoning in VLMs: patterns cannot be simulated reliably, yet physical verification is cheap and tangible. The author hand-crochets 40 patterns generated by four VLMs in the FoundationChain test, where models must infer from an image how an object was made and produce a matching pattern. Physical execution reveals failure modes invisible to paper-based evaluation, showing that convincing-looking procedures often do not work.
items.reasoning: A creative and rigorous grounded-evaluation methodology; the manual effort is impressive and the finding that plausible procedural outputs fail physically is broadly relevant for embodied and procedural reasoning, though the scale (40 patterns, one author) is small.

items.title: Beyond the Transcript: Measuring and Improving the Use of Acoustic Information in Audio Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.11573v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Audio language model benchmarks provide comprehensive evaluation across diverse tasks. However, some tasks can be answered from the transcript or even the question alone, and benchmark scores can therefore confound acoustic understanding with language modeling ability. We distinguish lexical tasks, for which the transcript usually suffices, from global-attribute and within-recording-structure tasks, which require the model to analyse the recording beyond its words, either as a whole, for properties such as the speaker and emotion, or within it, for patterns such as stress and intonation. We evaluated 19 open models and Gemini 3.1 Pro on 92 tasks from 6 benchmarks and estimated the recording gain, the accuracy advantage of the original recording over references that retain its words, by comparing the recording with synthetic readings of its transcript and by adding it to the transcript. On attribute and structure tasks, the open models fall behind Gemini by 28.6 and 41.9 percentage points, and about half or more of each deficit lies in the recording gain. Nevertheless, linear probes in Gemma-4 12B and Qwen2.5-Omni-7B show that the acoustic information needed for answering is already readable in early language-model layers, while the readout of many cues declines in the layers that follow. We therefore constructed training data and trained LoRA adapters in these layers, with a content anchor, which raises attribute and structure accuracy by 12.8 to 44.4 points in the two models and keeps mean lexical accuracy within 1 point of the base model. Most of the improvement appears as larger recording gains. These results suggest that training improves the use of acoustic information that the models already encode.

items.reasoning: A thoughtful evaluation-methodology contribution exposing transcript leakage in audio benchmarks, with broad coverage across models and tasks; includes an existing frontier model as reference rather than a new release, framing it as analysis of current capabilities.

items.title: Unlearning at Speed: Rapid Activation Dampening for Efficient Machine Unlearning in Real-World Face Recognition
items.content: arXiv:2611.11433v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Machine unlearning has become increasingly important in face recognition, where regulations like the GDPR empower users to request the removal of their personal data from deployed models. However, most existing unlearning methods are designed for closed-set classification with small-scale models and training data, and therefore do not generalize to real-world face recognition systems, which operate in an open-set setting with large-scale models and data. In this work, we propose Rapid Activation Dampening (RAD), a fast and targeted unlearning method tailored specifically for large-scale open-set face recognition. RAD approximates differences in average neuron activations between forget and retain identities, identifying and selectively suppressing neurons that are most associated with the targeted identity through a sensitivity-controlled dampening mechanism. We further propose the Forget Score (FS), which addresses the mismatch between existing unlearning metrics and open-set problems by providing a probabilistic interpretation of forgetting directly in the representation space. Experiments across several recent large-scale face recognition architectures and datasets show that RAD achieves strong forgetting while preserving overall model utility and substantially improving unlearning speed. These findings establish RAD as a scalable and practical approach to machine unlearning in face recognition systems.

items.summary: RAD is a fast, targeted machine unlearning method for large-scale open-set face recognition that approximates activation differences between forget and retain identities and selectively suppresses neurons, addressing the gap between closed-set unlearning research and deployed recognition systems. It is motivated by GDPR-driven data-removal requirements.
items.reasoning: Bridges a real regulatory-to-technical gap by adapting unlearning to open-set, large-scale recognition; the activation-dampening mechanism is simple but practical, and the deployment framing strengthens its significance.

items.title: DASH-SLAM: Calibration-Free Metric Monocular SLAM via Depth Scale Propagation
items.content: arXiv:2611.10239v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Geometric foundation models estimate dense geometry and camera parameters from monocular images, but reliable SLAM also requires consistent scale and accurate data association across successive reconstructions. We present DASH-SLAM, a monocular SLAM system that integrates metric depth predictions from pretrained Depth Anything 3 into a shared-keyframe pose graph without task-specific fine-tuning. DASH-SLAM derives scale corrections from depth ratios at shared anchor images and accumulates them across reconstructions, with a damping factor controlling their influence. These corrections rescale odometry translations, loop constraints, and map geometry. Experiments on TUM, Replica, and 7-Scenes show that DASH-SLAM outperforms state-of-the-art methods. We evaluate performance using both rigid and similarity alignment to distinguish metric-scale fidelity from accuracy up to scale. We further evaluate DASH-SLAM on four challenging sequences in perceptually-degraded environments from the Unified Autonomy Stack field dataset, covering tunnels, fog, and a frozen lake. On these sequences, DASH-SLAM outperforms the foundation-model SLAM state-of-the-art and maintains tracking where classical SLAM methods fail.

items.title: Explicitly capturing demonstrator multi-modality for distillation into diffusion policies
items.content: arXiv:2611.10949v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The diversity of a distilled diffusion policy's outputs matters beyond how it impacts the policy's success rate. In particular, downstream applications like test-time search and policy improvement require exploration. Thus, we want to distill multi-modal demonstrators into diffusion policies which reproduce their conditional action distributions. Standard data collection for behavior cloning applies a sliding window to demonstration episodes, which pairs unique observation histories with actions. These datasets can be fit by a policy that is either multi-modal, or unimodal with high Lipschitz constant to capture a diversity of actions seen at nearby observation samples. Prior work finds that diffusion policies trained on sparse data learn the latter, memorizing one action per observation. We adapt vine sampling to behavior cloning data collection to resolve this ambiguity: at some states the demonstrator visits, query it $k$ times from exactly the same observation. On a synthetic task, we study how the number of actions per observation, $k$, affects the learned policy, and find that larger $k$ yields a policy that better matches the demonstrator's conditional distribution, including its multi-modality and diversity. On a 2D truck unloading task, vine sampling likewise leads to a policy closer to the demonstrator and substantially improves both best-of-$N$ and expert iteration performance.
items.author: Shao Yuan Chew Chia, Rebecca H. Jiang, Abhinav Agarwal, Andreas Hofmann, Leslie Pack Kaelbling, Russ Tedrake
items.summary: This paper examines how to distill multi-modal demonstrators into diffusion policies that reproduce conditional action distributions, noting that sliding-window BC data can be fit either by a multi-modal policy or by a unimodal policy with high Lipschitz constant. The authors argue that output diversity matters for downstream applications like test-time search and policy improvement, and propose methods to explicitly capture demonstrator multi-modality.
items.reasoning: Conceptually rigorous analysis of an underappreciated aspect of diffusion policy distillation (output diversity beyond success rate), with implications for exploration and policy improvement; strong authors from MIT, but the work is a refinement of existing diffusion policy understanding.

items.title: D-REAL: Acceptance-Length Optimization with Unbiased Gradients for Speculative Decoding
items.content: arXiv:2611.10432v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Speculative decoding efficiency depends on the number of consecutively accepted draft tokens, yet token-level training objectives do not directly optimize this quantity. We introduce D-REAL (Drafter Reinforcement of Expected Acceptance Length), a post-training method that directly optimizes expected acceptance length for a fixed decoding context. D-REAL weights position-wise draft-target distributional overlap by prefix survival probabilities along a draft-sampled prefix, faithfully capturing the sequential dependence of verification on earlier proposals. By accounting for the parameter dependence of the proposal distribution, we derive an unbiased gradient estimator for this single-round objective under stochastic verification. We evaluate D-REAL on DSpark and DFlash2 with Qwen3-8B as the target model across ten benchmarks. Starting from baselines whose mean acceptance length has plateaued, one epoch of D-REAL post-training consistently improves the benchmark-averaged mean acceptance length by up to 0.23 tokens across both architectures under greedy (T = 0.0) and stochastic (T = 1.0) sampling, translating into up to a 9.4% end-to-end serving throughput improvement.
items.author: Meng Wei, Yefei Chen, Antong Li, Yanan Gao, Xingliang Shi, Xin Gao, Zhiling Ye, Yun Yue, Chunxiao Guo, Peng Wei
items.summary: D-REAL is a post-training method for speculative decoding drafters that directly optimizes expected acceptance length using a gradient estimator that accounts for prefix survival probabilities and stochastic verification, with an unbiasedness guarantee. It moves beyond token-level objectives that do not align with the actual efficiency metric. It matters because speculative decoding is widely deployed for fast LLM inference.
items.reasoning: Theoretically grounded contribution (unbiased gradient estimator for a nontrivial objective) to an important inference-efficiency problem. Practical relevance is high if gains transfer across model pairs, though the technique is a refinement rather than a paradigm shift.

items.title: RetinaGuard: Risk-Controlled Agentic Triage for Multi-Disease Retinal Screening
items.content: arXiv:2611.10689v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Retinal screening programmes need to know which automated decisions can be accepted without review. This paper presents RetinaGuard, an agentic triage framework in which quality, diagnostic, uncertainty, verification and explanation agents gather evidence for each fundus photograph, a learned failure predictor estimates the probability that the decision is unsafe, auxiliary tools are invoked only when their expected value of information exceeds their cost, and the acceptance threshold is certified by conformal risk control. On the RFMiD test split, RetinaGuard was compared with confidence and calibrated-uncertainty referral at matched referral budgets and equal certified safety, using two RETFound primary models of different strength. With the weaker model (macro-AUROC 0.896), verifier disagreement added significant information, RetinaGuard captured 119 of 280 unsafe decisions at a 20% budget against 88 for lowest-confidence referral, and at a nominal 5% unsafe level it accepted 37.0% of cases against 10.3%. With the stronger model (0.925) the verifier added nothing beyond uncertainty and the advantage shrank to a few percentage points. In both settings its coverage at the nominal 5% level stayed near 37.7%, gating cut computation by about 30%, and a quality agent reduced unsafe acceptances under most image corruptions. The benefit of agentic evidence gathering thus depends on how much the primary model's own uncertainty already reveals about its errors.

items.title: Hallucination-Guided Unlearning: Using Hallucination Traces to Reveal Overfitted Memories
items.content: arXiv:2611.10697v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Selective unlearning is increasingly important for the safety and compliance of large language models. Harmful or memorized content is often entangled with useful knowledge and difficult to enumerate. We use the model's own failures to identify candidates for unlearning. We propose Hallucination-Guided Unlearning (HGU), which uses hallucinations as diagnostic signals. HGU localizes unsupported spans via evidence and internal consensus, traces a sparse set of high-responsibility MLP neurons, and edits them with compact gates under a utility-preserving KL constraint. On TOFU, HGU achieves the best MU-FE trade-off, with Avg scores of 0.7221 (forget05) and 0.7699 (forget10), and the highest SepS H-Avg (0.4382/0.4715) under mixed forget/retain prompts. On the WMDP auxiliary task, HGU yields the strongest forgetting (e.g., 14.2 on Economics) while improving Retain (52.7) and MMLU (57.2). These results suggest that tracing hallucinations enables targeted, post-hoc unlearning that better balances forgetting efficacy and general utility without full retraining.

On TOFU it achieves the best MU-FE trade-off with reported Avg scores of 0.7221 and 0.7699 on forget05 and forget10 splits.

items.title: Lightfoot: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Exact, Model-Free Document Deletion
items.content: arXiv:2611.11010v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) improves multi-hop question answering, but deployed systems face two costs that research comparisons rarely measure: building the graph, and removing documents from it. We present Lightfoot, a GraphRAG system in which every entity, link, fact and synonym edge is a deterministic function of per-passage extractions carrying chunk-level provenance. Indexing makes one language-model call per passage, retrieval makes none, and deleting a document is a database operation with no model calls. On the full 11,402-passage MuSiQue corpus we verify that, after deleting 10% of the documents, the graph is identical to a fresh index of the surviving documents. We compare Lightfoot with HippoRAG 2, LightRAG and fast-graphrag under identical extraction, answer and embedding models on MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA. Lightfoot builds the cheapest index on all three datasets, 26-31% below HippoRAG 2 and 3-6x below LightRAG and fast-graphrag. Against HippoRAG 2 it is significantly better on MuSiQue retrieval (+2.8 points recall@5 and +4.3 recall@10 on a held-out split) and on HotpotQA answers (+7.7 points exact match), and significantly worse on 2WikiMultiHopQA (-3.9 recall@2, -8.4 F1). Deleting the same documents took LightRAG 2,187 model calls and 3.7 hours; fast-graphrag has no deletion path. Code and per-question results: https://github.com/udayallu-ml/Lightfoot-GraphRAG

items.title: Self-Indexing Latent Memories for Access-Aware Continual Instruction Tuning of LLMs
items.content: arXiv:2611.11684v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Continual instruction tuning often preserves old skills with task-private modules. Inference still requires selecting the right module from the prompt alone. We introduce Task-Isolated Latent Adapter Continual Training (TILA-CT), a replay-free method that makes each task module self-indexing. Each task receives a latent memory and adapter bank in a frozen LLM. During adaptation, the memory gathers causal-prefix information and injects task-conditioned context. For access, its persistent state provides the routing prototype used by a shared prompt-only router. On the 8-task CT-Pipeline stream, TILA-CT achieves 65.19 acquisition and 63.98 final macro score, with 1.38 points of average forgetting. A middle-reversed order gives 65.38 acquisition and 64.17 final macro score. Across 6 backbones, final scores remain within 1.5 points of acquisition. Ablations support memory-derived routing keys and causal gathering. Final macro routing accuracy is 93.9\%, and oracle routing recovers 1.21 final macro points. These results separate preserved task computation from learned access to it.

items.title: ACROSSVAM3.0: Resource-Bounded 4D Scene Construction and Adaptive Surface Association
items.content: arXiv:2611.11825v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Combining video generation, dynamic reconstruction and monocular SLAM requires consistent coordinates, explicit handling of missing outputs and predictable memory use. We present AcrossVAM3.0, an offline system that converts text, images or monocular RGB video into a versioned point representation. Frozen components run sequentially on one GPU; map corrections update cameras, points and trajectories together. The coordination layer adds no neural parameters. Three fresh input-mode runs completed with a maximum sampled task-process-tree GPU footprint of 17.14 GB. In a frozen 16-scene video suite, every scene yielded a 4D reconstruction and 15 yielded a non-empty SLAM map. Strict cross-window matching reduced local surface error but lost long-range track coverage on TAP-Vid-DAVIS. We therefore developed multi-hypothesis adaptive surface chaining (MHAC), which retains several candidate matches and an explicit missing state. After selection on disjoint development data, MHAC improved Average Jaccard over a position-only baseline by 0.1394 on a frozen ten-video holdout (95% bootstrap interval [0.1074,0.1689]). Across 265 RoboTAP videos, the mean paired gain was 0.0610 ([0.0510,0.0715]), with 215 wins, one tie and 49 losses. These results support resource-bounded scene construction and an external tracking gain under the tested protocol. They do not establish metric scale, semantic identity or high-fidelity novel-view rendering.

items.title: OGDA: Ontology-Grounded Data Agents for Reliable Analysis over Heterogeneous Data Lakes
items.content: arXiv:2611.12114v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Full-pipeline data analysis over real-world data lakes requires LLM agents to locate and integrate information across large collections of tables with different schemas. Existing data agents follow task-specific exploration, which exhausts the context window in massive lakes. As the context fills, the agent's reasoning degrades, leading it to locate and process incorrect data files. These errors propagate into the final answer. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Ontology-Grounded Data Agent (OGDA), which utilizes a compact ontology to reduce exploration overhead and constrain data processing. OGDA constructs the ontology through agentic hypothesis testing. At each step, a proposer agent induces schemas, concepts, and relations from raw sources, and a verifier checks each proposal against the underlying data. During task execution, the ontology serves as a representation of the data lake for the agent to explore. Every data-processing action is constrained by a task graph, which the agent can extend only after observing the semantic meaning of the data. Across KramaBench and DiscoveryBench with three LLM backbones, OGDA outperforms the strongest baselines by up to 10.82 points. These results suggest that explicitly modeling the data lake is a key step toward reliable end-to-end data agents.
items.author: Boyi Zhang, Hong Ting Tsang, Yisen Gao, Qiao Xiao, LI Yufei, Haoyu Huang, Zhongwei Xie, Jiaxin Bai, Yangqiu Song
items.summary: OGDA tackles LLM data agents running out of context on large heterogeneous data lakes by constructing a compact ontology through agentic hypothesis testing to constrain exploration and data processing. A proposer-critic style loop induces schemas, concepts, and relations, reducing the exploration overhead and error propagation that plagues task-specific exploration.
items.reasoning: A practical solution to a real failure mode of data agents at scale, with the ontology-grounding design being sensible and well-motivated. The approach is a useful engineering advance rather than a conceptual leap in agent capabilities.

items.title: ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents
items.content: arXiv:2611.12232v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: On-policy self-distillation lets a language agent act as its own Teacher by conditioning on privileged context such as skills written from its own trajectories. Its guidance, however, is weighted by how much this context shifts token likelihoods rather than by whether it improves behavior, so errors in self-written skills return through later updates. We propose environment-calibrated on-policy self-distillation, which uses environmental outcomes to decide how much to trust the Teacher's current guidance and which self-written skills to reinforce. Command-level advantages, estimated by comparing commands executed at similar observations, scale each Teacher preference and reward reflections and skills whose induced preferences favor higher-advantage commands. Without skills at inference, 3B and 7B agents reach 90.5% and 93.3% macro success on seen ALFWorld tasks and 75.5% and 80.5% success on WebShop. On unseen ALFWorld tasks, they outperform GRPO under the same protocol by 11.0 and 7.6 percentage points, respectively. In an ablation study, supervising only executable commands rather than the Actor's full response raises 3B WebShop success from 52.3% to 75.0%.

items.summary: ECOS improves on-policy self-distillation for language agents by using environmental outcomes to decide how much to trust a self-teacher's guidance and which self-written skills to reinforce. Command-level advantages, estimated by comparing commands executed at similar observations, scale teacher preferences so that harmful self-written skills do not propagate through later updates.
items.reasoning: Calibrating self-distillation with real environment outcomes addresses a known failure mode of privileged-context self-teaching, and the advantage estimation over similar observations is a thoughtful mechanism. It is an incremental refinement over an emerging self-distillation line rather than a new paradigm.

items.title: Detecting Shadow AI: Unsanctioned LLM Agents on Enterprise Endpoints: A Taxonomy, an Open Detector and a Controlled Evaluation
items.content: arXiv:2611.12377v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Shadow IT, the use of technology that the IT organisation has not approved, is a long-standing governance problem. We argue that autonomous AI agents can make it grow much faster: agents make building tools nearly free, act with their user's privileges, and leave behind scripts, automations and MCP servers that are themselves unsanctioned. A simple compounding model shows that, under its assumptions, shadow IT grows exponentially once agentic artifacts reproduce faster than the organisation retires them; retiring them starts with detecting them. We then ask whether unsanctioned agents can be detected on Windows endpoints. We propose a taxonomy of nine classes of agents and six layers of endpoint footprint, and argue that rules based only on the structure of processes and connections cannot separate an agent from its behavioural twin, the same program talking to a non-AI service. We present Agent Detector, an open-source Windows detector that anchors behaviour to the identity of the remote service and correlates it with configuration, installation and execution history, using a catalog of 39 tools and 184 LLM endpoint entries; it informs users through a notice they must acknowledge instead of blocking. On a controlled bench of 12 synthetic agents, 3 AI components and 9 benign workloads, repeated 5 times on one workstation, two behavioural rules flagged every behavioural twin, while Agent Detector flagged none and detected every agent in the majority of runs. Its limits are temporal: a connection to a provider behind a shared content-delivery network is attributable only while the DNS cache holds the provider's name, one to five minutes, and an intermittent agent was seen by about one scan in three. A scan costs about 154 ms. The bench is too small to rank detectors; it maps what each kind of evidence can see: unsanctioned agents can be partly detected, and not by behaviour alone.

It proposes a taxonomy of nine agent classes and six endpoint footprint layers, an open detector for Windows endpoints, and a controlled evaluation. This is a timely and practically important contribution to AI governance and security.

items.title: GMD-Mamba: Lightweight 3D Medical Image Segmentation Using a Grouped Multi-Directional Mamba
items.content: arXiv:2611.10032v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Mamba has the capability to capture global context in linear time for 3D medical image segmentation. However, existing methods employ Mamba with full-width directional scans at every resolution, keeping the model large (64-138M parameters and high FLOPs). We propose Grouped Multi-Directional (GMD) Mamba, a lightweight network based on the GMD scan that divides input channels $C$ into groups $G$ and flattens each group in different directions in one pass. This gives multi-directional context at $O(C^2/G)$ instead of $O(K \cdot C^2)$, where $K$ is the number of scan directions. Additionally, we employ Mamba only at the deepest encoder stages, resulting in 19.2M parameters. On BraTS2023, it achieves the best average Dice of 92.0% and the lowest HD95 of 2.7 at $\sim$1/7 the parameters of SegMamba-V2. For model validation, we also ran experiments on the MSD Spleen dataset, achieving competitive performance. The implementation details and code are publicly available at https://github.com/2802990u/GMD-Mamba.

The result is a 19.2M-parameter model achieving best average Dice of 92.0% on BraTS2023.

items.title: FAIR Universe Weak Lensing ML Uncertainty Challenge: Dataset and Cosmological Inference Competition
items.content: arXiv:2611.10228v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Weak gravitational lensing is a powerful cosmological probe that enables direct mapping of the matter distribution and precise constraints on the fundamental parameters governing structure formation in the universe. In recent years, machine learning has shown strong potential for extracting cosmological information from weak-lensing data beyond traditional summary statistics. However, progress has been limited by the lack of standardized benchmarks that capture the complexity of the dataset, simulator imperfections, and various systematic biases encountered in realistic analyses. To address this gap, we present the FAIR Universe Weak Lensing Machine Learning Uncertainty Challenge, one of the NeurIPS 2025 competitions, as a benchmark dataset and evaluation study. Our dataset reflects realistic weak-lensing observations, incorporating multiple systematic biases, and thereby providing a controlled testbed for robust cosmological inference under uncertainties. We summarize the main methodological advances developed by the winners of our challenge, including data augmentation with conditional optimal transport, an AI-agent-driven approach for parameter inference, ensemble learning, Vision Transformer-based architectures, and physics-informed feature integration. By unifying the benchmark dataset and the winning solutions, this work provides a community resource for developing and evaluating machine learning methods for weak lensing cosmology and, more broadly, for scientific inference under systematic uncertainties.

items.title: Track or Follow? A Jev-Compatible Multi-Agent Trading System When Web News Lags the Market
items.content: arXiv:2611.10414v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: LLM agents increasingly trade on the Web news they read, yet much Web news about listed firms is published after, and about, the price move it reports, so a reader can agree with the market by following it instead of reading the event. We ask whether LLM judgments of Web news track the market's reaction to the reported event or follow it. To answer, we built a multi-agent trading system whose agents share only point-in-time stores and answer typed questions through the interface of Jev, a hosted typed decision model; code sets every position under a proved bound on how far text can move it. In a hash-committed test of a Jev-compatible reader built from a pinned LLM's option probabilities, item judgments track announcement-window abnormal returns (weekly Spearman 0.119), also after the LLM's release, and event types agree with the issuers' 8-K filings (AUC 0.833); Jev's judgments of news published after its own release track the reaction as well (descriptive). Exploratory analyses show where the association comes from: 72% of earnings news items appear after the issuer's filing, contributor-written items often report the price move, and from the first trade after publication the association falls to 0.023. At a weekly horizon, the confirmatory test detects no rank information over code-only features. Under attack, decision cards traced 88% of successful attacks to the planted item. We propose that market-graded tests of Web-text readers report the criterion from publication, not only from the event.
items.author: Yebo Feng, Guangyan Gan, Liangrui Pan, Ruichao Liang, Cong Wu, Jiahua Xu, Yang Liu
items.summary: This paper asks whether LLM agents trading on web news actually predict market moves or merely echo reactions already priced in, since much financial news is published after the move it reports. The authors build a multi-agent trading system with point-in-time data stores and a typed decision model (Jev) with provable position bounds, showing judgments track announcement-window abnormal returns rather than anticipate them. It highlights a subtle look-ahead leakage problem in LLM-based finance applications.
items.reasoning: A carefully engineered study with an interesting epistemological question (track vs. follow) and unusual rigor (typed decision model with proved bounds, hash-committed tests), but niche application and less general methodology.
