items.title: Confusion-Adaptive Margin Learning for Handwritten Letter Recognition: A Controlled Study on EMNIST Letters
items.content: arXiv:2611.09953v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Handwritten character recognition systems can achieve high accuracy while retaining concentrated errors among visually similar classes. Motivated by residual letter confusions in earlier geometry-based recognition work, we investigate whether these errors can be addressed through the training objective. We introduce Confusion-Adaptive Margin Learning (CAML), which constructs a sparse weighted confusion graph from a discovery partition held out from pilot training and applies pair-specific cosine-separation constraints during final training. CAML adds no classifier, routing rule, or inference-time parameters.   We evaluate CAML on EMNIST Letters against a strictly matched cross-entropy CNN baseline, using the same architecture, final training data, deterministic augmentation, optimizer, and checkpoint selection. Eight confusion pairs are targeted: I/L, G/Q, U/V, R/V, D/O, C/E, I/J, and H/N. On the official clean test set, accuracy changes from 95.6346% to 95.6731%, and macro-F1 from 0.956326 to 0.956724. Mean accuracy across ten predefined corrupted conditions increases from approximately 95.3812% to 95.4303%; symmetric errors within targeted pairs decrease from 614 to 605 (1.47%).   The global differences are small and not statistically reliable. CAML fixes 124 baseline errors but introduces 116 new errors on clean data (exact McNemar p=0.6515), and no corruption-specific difference remains significant after Holm correction. Thus, CAML does not establish global superiority, but shows that a leakage-controlled, pair-specific margin objective can alter targeted error structure with limited overall benefit for an already strong classifier.

items.title: Rule-table structure of life-like cellular automata: activity, asymmetry, sensitivity, and the propagation storage factorisation
items.content: arXiv:2611.10969v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: What structure on the rule space of a cellular-automaton family exposes which rules can support which behaviours? For the 262,144 life-like rules -- the two-dimensional outer-totalistic family containing Conway's Game of Life -- the standard coordinate, Langton's activity parameter, is long known to be too coarse. I organise the family by three symmetry-derived rule-table coordinates: an unweighted activity, a birth-survival asymmetry (odd under the swap of birth and survival), and the Vichniac-Binder Boolean-derivative sensitivity in closed form, whose centre-bit component vanishes exactly on the centre-blind (B=S) submanifold. The cardinality coordinates lambda, delta are necessary but never sufficient to certify behaviour; the centre-bit sensitivity labels the B=S submanifold on which the paper's one exact exclusion holds. Combined with an exhaustive enumeration of every rule's compact gliders, still lifes and oscillators (three-by-three seed, period at most sixteen), they expose a hierarchical factorisation: the birth condition is a narrow gate deciding whether anything can propagate, the survival condition tunes storage, and every compact-glider-supporting rule is birth-light and survival-rich. One exclusion is exact: no B=S rule supports a compact glider at that footprint, proven by exhaustive enumeration and closing only for compact-footprint patterns -- 36 B=S rules ship at four-by-four seed and 40 at five-by-five. Two dynamical results frame the whole: glider-capable rules that random sampling never expresses show that capability is certifiable from the table while its expression is only estimable from dynamics; and every uncatalogued rule producing a richly Life-like ecology turns out to be a Conway or HighLife variant on the neighbour counts its trajectories actually visit.

The paper shows Langton's activity parameter is too coarse and that coordinate-based quantities are necessary but insufficient to certify behavior. It also introduces a propagation-storage factorization.

items.title: Developing a Street View Imagery Processing Pipeline for Building-Level Vacant House Assessment
items.content: arXiv:2611.11893v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Street view imagery (SVI) is widely used to audit urban environments remotely. Automated assessments usually assume that each image shows the target building clearly. In practice, an image may lack task-relevant evidence or show a neighboring house. If this goes unchecked, a model's score cannot show whether it judged the correct building. We present a reproducible SVI processing pipeline that makes image suitability and target identity explicit and checkable. We apply it to vacant house assessment in South Korea, using 10,311 images of 1,609 detached-house parcels. Task-suitability filtering adapts its criteria to image composition and administrative area. This keeps coverage even across areas. While keeping as many images as a single uniform filter, our filtering left 101 more parcels with a usable image. Target-house alignment identifies the parcel's house from camera metadata and parcel boundaries. It needs no building footprints or additional training. Alignment matched human labels for 85.6% of images, compared with 79.8% for the best simple rule. In vacancy classification, filtering and alignment raised AUROC from 0.684 to 0.719, but marking a different house in the same image still gave 0.709. Grad-CAM showed that the model often looked at areas outside the target house. Image suitability, target identification, and model evidence are therefore separate problems, and scores alone do not resolve them. Recording which images were used and which house was selected lets reviewers verify each assessment and can support human virtual audits.

items.title: Beating the Pool, Not the Game: A White-Box Equilibrium Agent for Language-Based Economic Games
items.content: arXiv:2611.10932v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We describe sudsho, a rule-based agent for the GLEE Competition that plays bargaining, negotiation, and persuasion with zero inference-time LLM calls. Games are scored as payoff percentiles against an empirical pool of prior play on the same configuration, so pool percentiles set our demand targets while clamped equilibrium shares bound demands and acceptance. Every move is a deterministic function of the visible state (persuasion mixing aside), so alignment is verified by replaying the post-freeze move log through the policy. Across 117,280 games the agent reached an overall rating of 2056 at $0 inference cost, and the account, ranked by its best agent (a same-policy replica), placed 26th of 71 ranked accounts. A replay against three frozen snapshots of the opponent pool credits the pool-aware clamp with 274 to 330 points of mean per-game bargaining rating, an effect that holds where logged opponent decisions fix the replay.

items.title: Quality-Governed Deep Learning Network for Brain Tumor MRI Segmentation
items.content: arXiv:2611.09998v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The segmentation of brain tumors from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is an essential step for computer-aided neuro-oncology, treatment planning and follow-up. While effective encoder-decoder representations are achieved by U-Net and Attention U-Net, the skip sections of the network can generate weak-contrast or noisy responses in the case of heterogeneous boundaries of the tumor. In this paper, we introduce a Quality-Governed Deep Learning Network (QGDL-Net) that can be used for binary tumor segmentation from FLAIR MRI slices. The proposed model is able to predict the slice quality based on contrast and SNR statistics and to fine-tune the encoder features prior to decoding by learnable quality gates. We used the 80:20 train-validation split for experiments with BraTS 2021. QGDL-Net achieved a Dice of 0.9747, IoU of 0.9506, precision of 0.9755, recall of 0.9739, F1 of 0.9747 and accuracy of 0.9982, outperforming U-Net and Attention U-Net. The EigenCAM maps and segmentation overlays provide better tumor localization and interpretable activation around the lesion regions.
items.author: Asifiqbal Saiyed, Nitesh Chilakala, Jimmy Joseph, Praneetha Goli, Rohini Maskar

The approach targets weak-contrast and noisy responses in U-Net-style skip connections on heterogeneous tumor boundaries.
items.reasoning: A reasonable but incremental medical imaging contribution: quality-aware gating on top of established U-Net variants, evaluated on standard train-validation splits of likely public data. The novelty is modest and the authors' team is small-scale, so the work is unlikely to shift the field.

items.title: Unmasking Four Knapsack Problems in the Traveling Thief Benchmark
items.content: arXiv:2611.12597v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The traveling thief problem (TTP) asks a thief to choose a tour and a packing together, and the benchmark of 9,720 instances of Polyakovskiy et al. (2014) is the standard test set for comparing TTP heuristics. We show that four of these instances are not TTP instances at all. Their files give a renting rate of 0.00, so the tour has no effect on the objective and each instance reduces to a 0-1 knapsack problem. One of them belongs to the 60 categorized instances on which new methods are usually compared, and on it five of nine published methods report exactly the same value. The cause is the format of the files, which keep the renting rate with two decimals, while the rule of the generator gives a rate close to 0.003 on these instances. The same rounding may shift the rate of 949 other instances by more than 1%. Since the tour and the packing used by the generator were not published, the original rates cannot be recovered. We therefore define new rates with the same rule, applied to a fully specified reference solution that we publish, and we show with a published heuristic that the corrected instances behave as TTP instances again. We also give reference results on the corrected instances and recommendations for future studies. Finally, we present ttplib, a new open-source Python library that loads any of the 9,720 instances, including the corrected ones, without downloading the whole benchmark.

items.summary: The authors show that four instances in the standard 9,720-instance Traveling Thief Problem benchmark are not TTP instances at all: a renting rate of 0.00, caused by two-decimal file formatting, makes the tour irrelevant and reduces them to 0-1 knapsack problems. One affected instance belongs to the 60 categorized instances commonly used for comparisons, where five of nine published methods report identical values. This is a valuable benchmark-integrity correction for the combinatorial optimization community.

Finally, we present ttplib, a new open-source Python library that loads any of the 9,720 instances, including the corrected ones, without downloading the whole benchmark.

items.title: A four-view smartphone video dataset of a robot-held flexible strip, with camera poses and a 3D LaGSplat baseline
items.content: arXiv:2611.09959v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: This note describes a multi-view video dataset of a deformable object driven by a measured input, with the measured pose of every camera, and a first 3D result obtained on it with LaGSplat. LaGSplat learns from video a low-dimensional latent state that is both the generalized coordinate of a learned dissipative Lagrangian and the conditioning variable of a Gaussian Splatting decoder; fitting the decoder in 3D calls for synchronized multi-view footage, which the original paper only had from synthetic renderings. Here a robot arm moves a flexible strip by oscillating along a one-dimensional path, and four iPhones, three fixed and one handheld, film it for ten minutes. The videos are synchronized, the cameras are posed from the scene, and the position of the gripper is given per frame as the input of the system. LaGSplat fitted on this data with the gripper acceleration as a forcing term renders held-out views at 26 to 33 dB PSNR and runs as a real-time interactive demo in a web browser. Dataset, checkpoints and training code are public.

items.title: An Adaptive, Context-Aware, and Stacked Attention Network-Based Recommendation System to Capture Users' Temporal Preference
items.content: arXiv:2611.11278v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Recommendation systems have become more important since the widespread use of the Internet. The large amount of information means that it is difficult for users to discover they really need. However, users' preferences can change over time because of the age and the impact of social networks. Recommendation systems must capture users' preferences and recommend suitable items, which is a difficult challenge. This study proposes a novel recommendation system that adapts to the changing preferences of users. By learning and adapting to users' changing preferences better recommendations are provided. This study uses context factors as additional information to model users' preferences more precisely. For the proposed recommendation system, the context is based on users' interaction items within each defined time interval. This study proposes two novel attention mechanisms for the recommendation system. The contextual item attention module captures contextual information, changing pattern in users' preference and the importance of items. The multi-head attention module extends the diversity of users' preferences and adapts to changing preferences. The recommendation performance is improved using additional item's temporal information to model the contextual item's representation. Experiments compare the proposed algorithm with several state-of-the-art recommendation methods using three real-world datasets. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed context-aware recommendation model outperforms traditional methods and demonstrate the effectiveness with which contextual information is captured by the attention mechanism.

items.summary: Proposes a stacked attention-based recommendation system that models changing user preferences over time using contextual factors as additional signals. Claims improved recommendations by adapting to temporal preference drift.
items.reasoning: Incremental work in a crowded recommendation-systems space; the abstract suggests standard architectural combinations (attention stacking, context features) without clear evidence of significant novelty or strong benchmark gains.

items.title: From Sound to Occupancy: Privacy-Aware Audio Sensing for Buildings
items.content: arXiv:2611.11564v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Occupancy-based controls regulate lighting and HVAC according to whether a space is in use. Passive infrared (PIR) sensors, the most common choice, respond to motion and can report an occupied room as vacant when its occupants remain still. Sound offers an alternative cue, since seated occupants type, turn pages and cough, but microphones raise privacy concerns. We therefore study a two-stage design: an on-device encoder maps each second of audio to a short embedding, and a server-side temporal model turns the stream of embeddings into an occupancy state. To our knowledge, no publicly available dataset pairs office audio with occupancy labels, so we evaluate the two stages separately on public data. The encoder is trained on synthetic scenes that mix empty-room recordings, room impulse responses, office sounds and read speech, and tested on unseen rooms, recordings and speakers for whether a second contains a sound made by a person. On 11 real office recordings (DCASE 2013) it reaches an AUC of 0.87, against 0.76 for log-mel statistics. Attacks on the transmitted embeddings recover at most 1% of the spoken words, against 94% from log-mel frames, but still identify the speaker among 40 in 69 to 77% of the utterances. Noise-floor normalization with adversarial training, an 8-dimensional embedding, or sending only class probabilities lowers this to 38 to 55% without hurting detection. On HPDmobile, which pairs home occupancy labels with an amplitude envelope of the audio, a causal temporal model pretrained with a hierarchical contrastive loss matches hand-crafted features (AUC 0.75) and does better when only one labelled day per home is available. These results make the two-stage design a practical basis for privacy-aware acoustic occupancy sensing, with speaker identity as the one leak still to close.

items.title: Tutorial: Vision-Based Formation Control with Differential-Drive Robots
items.content: arXiv:2611.11164v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This tutorial presents a step-by-step introduction to multi-robot formation control using differential- drive robots, an overhead camera, and Python. ArUco markers are used to estimate robot positions and orientations, while desired pairwise displacement vectors define a circular formation. By comparing measured and desired relative positions, the controller computes movement vectors that are converted into differential-drive wheel commands, with basic proximity-sensor-based obstacle avoidance. The tutorial guides readers through hardware and software setup, robot pose estimation, formation geometry, feedback control, system integration, and formation-error evaluation. Motivated by the need to bridge the gap between theoretical understanding and practical implementation in robotics education, we emphasize how mathematical concepts are translated into coordinated behaviors on physical robots. Although the implementation uses a specific robotic platform, the underlying perception and formation-control principles can be adapted to other differential-drive robots and simulation environments. The accompanying open-source GitHub repository provides the Python implementation, setup instructions, and demonstrations to support hands-on learning and further exploration of multi-robot systems.

items.title: Objective Diversification of Dynamic Hedging
items.content: arXiv:2611.10333v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: A hedging objective reflects the risk preference of the hedger, so the conventional approach is to estimate the hedge ratio directly under the chosen objective. This paper asks whether that estimate should be used alone. We construct five objective-specific rolling hedge-ratio estimators---minimum variance, least absolute deviation (LAD), downside semivariance, lower-tail quantile, and Expected Shortfall (ES)---from the same historical stock--market returns, and combine the resulting estimates under a fixed final evaluation objective. Separate multi-output ExtraTrees models predict the within-stock-date ranks of the five candidates under MSE, LAD, downside semivariance, and 10\% quantile loss. The design uses pre-specified 60-, 90-, 120-, and 180-day windows with objective-matched rolling estimators as benchmarks. Adaptive weighting improves the corresponding loss in all sixteen objective--window comparisons. Equal weighting, which uses the same objective-specific hedge ratios without state variables or learned reweighting, already improves downside and quantile hedging. The results therefore suggest that estimates generated under other objectives can be useful even when the final hedging preference and evaluation objective are fixed, while adaptive weighting can provide a further improvement.

items.summary: Proposes combining five objective-specific rolling hedge-ratio estimators (minimum variance, LAD, downside semivariance, lower-tail quantile, expected shortfall) using multi-output ExtraTrees models that predict candidate rankings under different loss functions. The empirical finance study tests whether a diversified ensemble of hedge objectives beats any single-objective estimate. It is a domain-specific methodological contribution to dynamic hedging practice.

items.title: Smartphone-Enabled Depth-Aware Transillumination Imaging for Detection of Chicken Breast Fillet Myopathies in Chicken Fillets
items.content: arXiv:2611.12796v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Woody Breast (WB) myopathy is a major quality defect in broiler chickens characterized by fibrosis, increased tissue hardness, and altered structural properties that affect product quality. Conventional palpation is subjective and labor-intensive, while many non-destructive methods require specialized equipment or substantial computational resources. This study developed a smartphone-based transillumination and 3D point-cloud framework for non-destructive WB severity classification. A total of 267 chicken breast fillets, including normal breast (NB, n = 87), mild WB (MWB, n = 85), and severe WB (SWB, n = 95), were evaluated using RAW transillumination images and 3D point clouds acquired with an iPhone 16 Pro. A total of 91 features, comprising 14 image-derived, 76 geometric, and one physics-informed Beer-Lambert attenuation feature, were extracted. Partial correlation controlling for thickness revealed a significant association between image characteristics and WB severity (r = 0.413, p < 0.0001), indicating optical information independent of fillet geometry. SWB tissue exhibited approximately 26% greater light attenuation per unit thickness than NB. The 2D-only models achieved approximately 82% test accuracy, while the multimodal ensemble combining Fusion-DGCNN, XGBoost, and physics-guided logistic regression (PGLR) achieved approximately 90% accuracy. These findings demonstrate the complementary value of optical, geometric, and physics-informed features and establish the feasibility of smartphone-based, non-destructive WB severity assessment.

items.title: Writer-independent handedness identification from offline Bangla handwriting under controlled acquisition
items.content: arXiv:2611.10744v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Handedness is a soft-biometric cue for forensic document examination and writer profiling, yet reported accuracies from offline handwriting rarely keep writers, texts and image acquisition apart, so models may recognise the writer or capture conditions rather than the writing hand. Such controlled evidence is missing for Bangla. Using our BanglaHand dataset of 42 writers (21 left- and 21 right-handed), who each wrote six shared prompts and two own texts under controlled collection and photography, we evaluate handedness identification with all images of each test writer held out, whole-writer permutation tests and photometric controls. An ink-gradient descriptor identified the handedness of unseen writers with 77.4% balanced accuracy (95% writer-bootstrap interval 67.7-86.5%; p=0.001) and frozen ImageNet embeddings with 69.5-72.0%. Part of this signal is stroke darkness: in a post hoc analysis, right-handed writers' strokes were darker at their centres for equal stroke width, consistent with higher pen pressure and not explained by lighting drift. With ink density and brightness regressed out, the descriptor still reached 64.5% (p=0.027), whereas writing-only shape features were weaker (60.8%; p=0.090). Handedness is thus identifiable from offline Bangla handwriting under controlled acquisition, and photometric controls are essential to interpret such cues.

An ink-gradient descriptor achieves 77.4 percent balanced accuracy on unseen writers, with whole-writer permutation tests and photometric controls to avoid confounds. The work targets forensic document examination and writer profiling.

items.title: ROS2MR: Connecting ROS 2 Motion Planning to Mixed-Reality Trajectory Visualization
items.content: arXiv:2611.11830v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Mixed reality (MR) allows users to inspect planned robot motion within their physical surroundings, but displaying trajectories from robotics software requires converting their joint configurations and timing into a format the MR application can play back. This paper presents ROS2MR, an extension of the MR-Robotics LAB platform that converts YAML-serialized ROS 2 joint trajectories, including MoveIt motion plans, into the platform's existing JSON playback format. The converter validates the input, maps arm joints by name, and resamples the trajectory at a nominal rate of 30 Hz, using cubic Hermite interpolation when joint velocities are supplied and linear interpolation otherwise, while binary gripper commands are sampled separately using a zero-order hold. A Python export helper combines sequences of motion plans and gripper states into a single trajectory and checks positional agreement at segment boundaries. The MR application was also adapted for Apple Vision Pro in addition to Meta Quest 3. A technical evaluation showed that the converter preserved the normalized duration and endpoint configurations for dense, sparse, and irregularly timed inputs. With supplied velocities, the position RMSE was approximately 2.91x10^-5 degrees for all sampling patterns; without them, sparse input increased it to 0.85 degrees, and close positional agreement did not guarantee accurate velocity profiles. A pick-and-place sequence retained its open--closed--open gripper order, although off-grid transitions were shifted to the output sampling grid. The resulting file-based pathway enables inspection of ROS-generated trajectories in MR without a live ROS connection.

It handles validation, joint-name mapping, 30 Hz resampling with cubic Hermite or linear interpolation, and separate gripper command sampling. This is a practical systems contribution that lowers the barrier to inspecting planned robot motion in physical surroundings.

items.title: The Holographic Entropy Bound
items.content:
2.6.0 Here I'll briefly review some other aspects of physics that seem possibly important in supporting life and complexity, but which aren't quite as central to the main story I'm telling. This subsection is a bit of a grab bag.

## 2.6.1 Time, Space, Locality

2.6.1.1 Some rather obvious features of our world: we live in a universe with time, space, and local interactions, i.e. when evolving in time, the state of a given region is determined by some local neighbourhood of the region.

2.6.1.2 These are features we share with the Game of Life and other cellular automata, so they don't explain why we don't live there, although they do differentiate us from other mathematical structures.

2.6.1.3 Time seems necessary for something like life to exist, period. After all, what is life if it doesn't try to change or optimize its surroundings, which definitionally implies some sort of ability to affect other things, i.e. they are a function of the life-form's decisions, i.e. they are in its future. Whereas things that a life-form perceives are in its past.

- 2.6.1.3.1 There are subtleties here related to the low-entropy initial conditions and the retroactive nature of quantum branching. More on this later.

2.6.1.4 As for space, we're very used to it because we live here, but it's worth appreciating how much complexity and ability to create useful structures comes "for free" from living in 3D space. Padlocks and proteins are good examples (but really, you can probably look at anything around you and see this).

- 2.6.1.4.1 Sokoban puzzles are a fun way to see how even the most primitive notions of space (pushing blocks on a 2D grid) can give rise to extremely intricate and complex interactions. The Game of Life is another example, of course.

Figure: Locks and proteins are examples of the complex structures that can be created in 3D space. From here and here....

items.summary: An installment of an ongoing LessWrong series on conditions for life and complexity, reviewing physics fundamentals such as time, space, locality, and the holographic entropy bound, and asking why we do not live in cellular-automata-like worlds. The author connects locality and time to the prerequisites for life and discusses subtleties around low-entropy initial conditions and quantum branching. It is speculative physics-adjacent commentary within a larger intellectual project.

2.6.0 Here I'll briefly review some other aspects of physics that seem possibly important in supporting life and complexity, but which aren't quite as central to the main story I'm telling. This subsection is a bit of a grab bag.

2.6.1 Time, Space, Locality

2.6.1.1 Some rather obvious features of our world: we live in a universe with time, space, and local interactions, i.e. when evolving in time, the state of a given region is determined by some local neighbourhood of the region.

2.6.1.2 These are features we share with the Game of Life and other cellular automata, so they don't explain why we don't live there, although they do differentiate us from other mathematical structures.

2.6.1.3 Time seems necessary for something like life to exist, period. After all, what is life if it doesn't try to change or optimize its surroundings, which definitionally implies some sort of ability to affect other things, i.e. they are a function of the life-form's decisions, i.e. they are in its future. Whereas things that a life-form perceives are in its past.

  • 2.6.1.3.1 There are subtleties here related to the low-entropy initial conditions and the retroactive nature of quantum branching. More on this later.

2.6.1.4 As for space, we're very used to it because we live here, but it's worth appreciating how much complexity and ability to create useful structures comes "for free" from living in 3D space. Padlocks and proteins are good examples (but really, you can probably look at anything around you and see this).

  • 2.6.1.4.1 Sokoban puzzles are a fun way to see how even the most primitive notions of space (pushing blocks on a 2D grid) can give rise to extremely intricate and complex interactions. The Game of Life is another example, of course.

Figure: Locks and proteins are examples of the complex structures that can be created in 3D space. From here and here....

items.title: Spectrogram-Based CNN Autoencoder for One-Class Anomaly Detection in Machining Vibration Signals
items.content: arXiv:2611.10733v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This work presents a one-class anomaly detection framework for vibration-based condition monitoring in machining processes using a convolutional neural network autoencoder. Three-axis vibration signals acquired during industrial broaching are transformed into time--frequency spectrograms and combined into a compact three-channel representation, enabling convolutional feature learning on multivariate time-series data. The autoencoder is trained exclusively on normal process data and detects anomalous strokes based on reconstruction errors. Labeled validation data are used for threshold calibration and an independent test set is reserved for final performance evaluation. To improve sensitivity to short-lived process instabilities such as chatter, a localized residual-based metric termed Segmented Vertical Error (SVE) is introduced. Experimental results on approximately 10{,}000 broaching strokes show a clear separation between normal and anomalous process conditions under strong class imbalance. The processing pipeline is additionally evaluated on an external public turning dataset as a proof of concept, indicating preliminary applicability beyond the original broaching setup. The results suggest that spectrogram-based autoencoder models can provide a practical and scalable basis for one-class anomaly detection in industrial vibration monitoring.

items.title: Single Image Super-Resolution via Semantic Prompt and Cross-Modal Training on Content Area
items.content: arXiv:2611.12025v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Enhancing image quality through super-resolution is crucial in image and video processing. While contemporary deep learning models, such as CNNs and Transformers, excel in pixel-level enhancements, they often overlook the rich semantic context within images. To address this, we introduce a novel approach that synergizes pixel intensity with semantic information for superior detail recovery. Our method involves extracting semantic data, including textual descriptors and spatial positioning, and encoding this information. We also present a Cross-Modal Feature Fusion module for generating semantic feature maps via multimodal training, and a Prompt Traction Head to augment the backbone network with semantic insights, thereby refining image details. Our empirical results across various datasets validate the superiority of our approach.

items.summary: This single-author paper proposes a super-resolution approach that fuses pixel intensity with semantic information, using textual descriptors and spatial positioning encoded through a Cross-Modal Feature Fusion module and a Prompt Traction Head that augments the backbone with semantic cues for detail recovery.

Limited author context and scope further reduce expected impact.

items.title: Predictive Modelling of Solid Waste Generation through Time Series Analysis
items.content: arXiv:2611.10579v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Reliable forecasting of Municipal Solid Waste (MSW) production is pivotal for sustainable urban management, as it enables efficient resource planning, optimized collection schedules, and reduced environmental impacts. Existing works on MSW forecasting have some limitations, such as unavailability of granular data from lower administrative units, small datasets, limited or sometimes no consideration of important factors that can affect MSW generation, including holidays, weekends, seasonality, changes in temperature or humidity.   This work presents a comprehensive comparative analysis of four popularly used time series forecasting models, namely Seasonal Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average with Exogenous Regressors (SARIMAX), Prophet, Long Short Term Memory (LSTM) and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), using a real-world MSW dataset from Sri Lanka spanning 2012-2018. A detailed factor-wise analysis is conducted to examine waste generation behaviour considering holidays, weekday-weekend variations, seasonal patterns, temperature and humidity. The results show lower waste generation during holidays and weekends, higher generation during Summer and Winter, and comparatively lower generation during Monsoon and Post-Monsoon. Temperature and humidity do not exhibit a direct linear relationship with waste generation, although their seasonal variations are associated with the changes in waste generation across different seasons. All model performances are evaluated using Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE), Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), and the coefficient of determination (R2). Among the evaluated models, LSTM and SARIMAX achieve the best overall forecasting performance.

items.summary: A comparative study of time series forecasting models (SARIMAX, Prophet, and others) for municipal solid waste prediction, incorporating factors like holidays, seasonality, and weather. The work targets better urban resource planning and collection scheduling.
items.reasoning: A competent applied comparison of well-established forecasting methods on a domain-specific problem. Limited novelty in ML technique; value is mainly practical for sustainability and municipal management rather than advancing the field.

items.title: KR A1: Design and Preliminary Evaluation of a Humanoid-Robot Interaction Prototype Integrating Personalized Voice Synthesis, Contextual Dialogue, and Emotion-Aware Response Generation
items.content: arXiv:2611.09900v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: This paper presents the design and preliminary evaluation of KR A1, a humanoid-robot interaction prototype that integrates personalized voice synthesis, contextual dialogue processing, and emotion-aware response generation for potential mental-healthcare applications. The system architecture combines a locally hosted large language model (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, served via Ollama) for natural-language understanding and response generation, OpenVoice v2 for zero-shot speaker-adaptive speech synthesis, and a two-tier emotion-processing pipeline comprising a keyword heuristic and LLM-based inference. Face recognition (InsightFace) and vector memory retrieval (FAISS with sentence-transformer embeddings) enable user-personalized interaction. The experimental evaluation reported here is limited to the voice-cloning component: cloned voices were evaluated against reference recordings using eight acoustic similarity measures - mel-frequency cepstral coefficients, pitch, spectral centroid, spectral contrast, spectral rolloff, zero-crossing rate, formants, and speaker-embedding cosine similarity - supplemented by a same-speaker versus cross-speaker baseline comparison. All tests were conducted on a small, informal development sample; no statistical significance testing against a held-out baseline was performed. The emotion-recognition accuracy, end-to-end response latency, and therapeutic or clinical impact of the integrated system have not yet been formally evaluated and are identified as directions for future work. All testing was informal and self-conducted by the development team; no patients or external human participants were involved, and the system has not been evaluated or deployed in a clinical setting.

The paper reports only preliminary evaluation of the integrated system. It illustrates assembling off-the-shelf components into an empathetic companion robot.

items.title: An LLM-Orchestrated Multi-Modal Chatbot for Tomato Disease Consultant
items.content: arXiv:2611.10608v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This paper introduces a chatbot developed to assist in diagnosing common diseases in tomato plants through natural language interaction. Users can describe symptoms in text. Then, the chatbot responds with the most likely disease, and basic treatment suggestions and related image-based reasoning. The system leverages pre-trained Mistral and Llama 3.2 large language models. The system is also built using LangChain and Streamlit to provide a lightweight and offline-friendly interface. This work targets to support tomato growers a fast and accessible tomato plant health guidance when the technical expertise is not available nearby, especially in the remote areas. The experimental results are promising and encourage further improvement of the chatbot for future real-world deployment.

items.summary: This paper describes a chatbot for tomato disease diagnosis combining text symptom descriptions with image-based reasoning, built on pre-trained Mistral and Llama 3.2 models with LangChain and Streamlit for a lightweight offline-friendly interface aimed at growers in remote areas. items.title: A Strict Upper Bound for Three-Point Weighted Selection in Planar Vector-Valued Regression
items.content: arXiv:2611.12550v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We prove $F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(2,2,3)<11/6$ for minimum-Frobenius-norm least-squares regression with two input and two output coordinates, improving the upper bound $15/8$. More precisely, a universal $\varepsilon_0>0$ satisfies $\mathcal T_3\le(5/6-\varepsilon_0)E$ for every finite residual frame. The proof combines an exact scalar certificate, rigidity of equality in planar selection, and a compactness argument that controls disappearing weights. Together with the known lower bound, this gives $13/8\le F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(2,2,3)<11/6$. No numerical value of $\varepsilon_0$ is claimed.
items.author: Sergey Volkov
items.summary: This paper proves a strict upper bound F_weighted(2,2,3) < 11/6 for minimum-Frobenius-norm least-squares regression with two input and two output coordinates, improving the previous 15/8 bound. The proof combines an exact scalar certificate, rigidity of equality in planar selection, and a compactness argument controlling vanishing weights. Combined with known lower bounds this narrows the constant to a short interval.
items.reasoning: A rigorous and self-contained mathematical result, but it is an extremely specialized constant-tightening in approximation theory with little evident connection to broader AI research.

items.title: Would you press the button? The hard problem of alignment
items.content:
There is a TL;DR at the end.

The heaven button: You wake up one day and find a button in front of you, with a proof next to it. The proof says that pressing the button will kill everyone on the planet and send them all to heaven. Would you press it?

It seems too good to be true. You think it must be a dream. It can't possibly be true. You go through the proof, and it seems correct. But what if you were under the influence of some drug?

But the stakes are very high, so you use software you trust to formalize it in Lean, and you run it on a machine you trust. Lean says the proof is correct so now you are more convinced. But you start doubting yourself again. What if someone compromised the formalization software, or introduced a bug in Lean?

So you check Lean's code, and run the proof on a second machine with an independent checker. It passes again. But each of these checks could fail in the same way the first one could. So you go further and formally verify Lean and the formalization software themselves. They pass. But now you are doubtful of the tool you used to verify this. What if that was compromised by someone? Every new check needs another check behind it, and at some point you have to stop and decide.

Would you press it?

A common belief in AI labs and AI safety is that handing control to some general superintelligence would be fine, if we have a formal proof of alignment. That, in my opinion, is saying yes to the same button, except there is no proof yet, only the hope of one.

In this post, I present what I think is the hard problem of alignment.

- First, I illustrate why testing for alignment is not enough and a proof would be required.
- Then I lay out why a proof could be intractable.
- Finally, I argue that even a formal proof that a superintelligence is aligned does not justify its development.

## The hard problem of alignment...

The author uses this to argue that trust in verification chains is never fully grounded, connecting this to the hard problem of alignment and why buggy AI is harder to define and solve than buggy code. It is reflective commentary rather than original research.

items.title: Towers of Agency
items.content:
There is basically one reason to build a tower, and that’s access: There is something that is available higher up that is not available on the ground. Most commonly, that thing is either “empty space” or “information transmission”. A skyscraper can access more space than a shorter building, and so it fits more real estate in a smaller footprint. A watchtower can access strategic information from the land below; a church steeple is tall enough for the sound of the bells to travel far through the air. Many of the tallest structures in the world maximize line-of-sight for radio transmissions.

Imagine a stone or brick tower of your favorite type - one whose purpose is to access something high up. Or, if you prefer a specific suggestion, imagine the brick steeple of Old North Church in Boston, which held the signaling lanterns for Paul Revere.

Consider some unremarkable block in the tower: On either side of this block are other blocks. Sitting on top of this block are more blocks. Below, holding our block’s weight: more blocks.

One can ask, about the block we’ve chosen, the question “how?”: How is it that this block is at this spot? And the answer to that question is, locally, that it is held up by other blocks immediately below. Those blocks depend on others below them, and so indirectly our block is here by the grace of the whole set of blocks transitively beneath it.

One can ask, about the block we’ve chosen, the question “why?”: For what purpose is this block at this spot? And the answer to that question is, locally, that it is holding up other blocks immediately above. Those blocks are holding up others above them, and so indirectly our block is here in order to help hold up the whole set of blocks transitively above it....
items.author: benwr
items.summary: A conceptual essay using towers as a metaphor for agency: towers exist to access something unavailable at ground level, whether space or information transmission, and each block in a tower is supported by layers below. The author uses this framing to reason about how capability and support structures stack, connecting physical intuition to questions about agency. It is a reflective piece rather than empirical or formal work.

items.title: All Interesting Behavior Is Overdetermined
items.content:
This is an essay about individual rationality technique. It's intended to show that "All interesting behavior is overdetermined" is, under a specific meaning of "overdetermined" that is stronger than just "multicausal", a valuable heuristic for generative understanding and the avoidance of error.

Scott Alexander's 2018 essay The Omnigenic Model As Metaphor for Life is a clear statement of what has become general rationalist doctrine on multicausality. Scott observed that behavioral genetics was difficult because complex human traits involved far more interacting causes than workers expected. He draws this methodological lesson: “We should go from trying to discover ‘the’ cause, to trying to find out which factors we need to create the best polycausal model.” He applies the same reasoning to depression, intelligence, comma, and other complex psychological phenomena. He explicitly warns against looking for one or ten causes when there might be dozens or hundreds.

Scott is, however, talking mainly about contributory causation, when an effect is produced by an accumulation of causes; in his type example, there are probably twenty thousand genes which contribute to intelligence, but no one "intelligence gene". This is not quite the same as overdetermination, which describes a situation in which a complex behavior could be explained with any one of multiple causes, each one in itself sufficient.

When we find a sufficient explanation, or a sufficiently good collection of contributory explanations like Scott's 20,000 genes, there's a strong tendency to think that we can stop there. The rest of this essay is about why we shouldn't....
items.author: Eric Raymond
items.summary: An essay on individual rationality technique by Eric Raymond arguing that interesting behavior is overdetermined in a stronger sense than merely multicausal, building on and extending Scott Alexander's omnigenic-model metaphor. It develops a heuristic for generative understanding and error avoidance in analyzing complex causes.
items.reasoning: A thoughtful rationality-community essay, but it is general epistemics with no AI-specific content, models, or experiments, so its relevance to AI research analysis is minimal.

When we find a sufficient explanation, or a sufficiently good collection of contributory explanations like Scott's 20,000 genes, there's a strong tendency to think that we can stop there. The rest of this essay is about why we shouldn't....

items.title: Preservation can save the world!
items.content:
I'm Aurelia Song and I founded the preservation company Nectome. We do planned whole-body end-of-life preservation for future revival. That is, terminally-ill people come to us in Oregon, and we preserve them immediately after their death in the hopes that one day people in the future will welcome them back with love. We want to build a future that celebrates and restores those who are preserved today. I've argued at length in previous posts that properly done end-of-life preservation works today because we know structural preservation is sufficient and we can provably preserve sufficient structure. This post is about some of the consequences of this being true.

### Perhaps surprisingly, I think end-of-life preservation is extremely relevant in the next year to getting AI right. I'm writing this post to directly state my case, since I haven't seen it expressed clearly before.

tl;dr: Preservation offers a much safer option to those accelerationists who are rushing to AI in the hopes of saving the lives of people they love who have only a few years to live. Those people can be preserved, so there's no need to rush anymore. Preservation gives everyone a place of psychological safety from which we can all work to do AI right even if it will take slightly longer. That's why it's important, today.

# How could preservation possibly be relevant to AI this year?

You may think, "what's the point of preservation, even if it works? The only thing that matters is AI! If we get AI right, we will enter a utopia and cure all diseases and preservation won't matter because no one will need it. If we don't get AI right, preservation also won't matter because the AI will kill every living person and destroy every preserved person in its quest to pursue its mad goals. Either way, getting AI right is the only thing that matters and everything else, including preservation, is just a distraction."...

items.title: Don't rely on EV, especially if you only have one life
items.content:
You are offered a lottery by a man on the street:

Option A - 100% chance to win 50 dollars (EV: +50)

Option B - 80% chance to win 100 dollars, 20% chance to lose 20 dollars (EV: +76)

You choose option B. It has more than 1.5 times the EV of option A! The man rolls a 100-sided die.

It comes up 6. You lose 20 dollars, he laughs and walks away.

You only have one life. EV calculations work best in frequentist worlds, worlds where you get to experience a particular choice over and over again. This might happen if you're choosing which route to take to work every day, or what restaurant to visit in your neighbourhood. However, these choices are the exception. The vast majority of choices in life, especially the important ones, are only offered once.

There are some frameworks which offer answers to these questions, including models that give diminishing marginal utility to money or maximise the geometric expectation. But these models work best when you can fit a number onto your outcome. In every choice you will be offered, the outcomes are usually far more rich and varied than simple monetary reward and loss (which is itself sensitive to your economic position, outstanding debts/obligations, necessary immediate expenditures...). While unlikely outcomes may contribute small amounts to your EV, they may contribute large amounts to your subjective experience. Often, people who commit crimes don't think they will get caught.

And that's the thing, isn't it? For choices that only come up once in your life, you have very little primary or secondary knowledge to construct your odds. Things that seem foolproof often are not, and volatility usually hurts you more than it helps. Decision theories only work if the payout matrices are clear, and making them clear is half the battle. This is why maintaining personal rules and standards in the face of uncertainty is important.

You have many years to live - do things you will be proud to remember when you're old....

items.title: Be less scared of overconfidence
items.content:
When I was deciding whether to work for Wave, I got very hung up on the fact that my “total compensation” would be “lower.”

The scare quotes are there because Wave and my previous employer, Theorem, were both early-stage startups that were paying me mostly in fake startup bucks equity. To figure out the total compensation, I tried to guess how much money the equity in each company was worth, with a thought process something like:

- Both of these companies have been invested in by reputable, top-tier venture capitalists.

- The market for for-profit investments is pretty efficient, and most people who think they can do better are being overconfident.

- Who am I, a lowly 22-year-old programmer, to disagree with reputable top-tier venture capitalists? I should defer to them about the valuations.

So I valued the equity by taking the valuation each company’s VCs had invested at, and multiplied it by the fraction of the company my shares represented. That number was higher for Theorem than for Wave.

Seven years on, the Wave equity turned out to be… a lot more valuable. That raises the question: how dumb was my take? Was the actual outcome predictable if I’d thought about it in the right way?

I don’t think it was perfectly predictable, but I do think I shouldn’t have been that anchored to the market-efficiency reasoning. Those respectable, top-tier VCs had YOLOed those valuations after a couple one-hour meetings, because that’s how early-stage VC works. Meanwhile, I had worked at Theorem for a year and my then-partner had worked at Wave for nine months. Heck, I had gotten more founder time than those VCs had just during my interview process. I had way more information than “the market.”

If I’d had the confidence to use that information, I might have thought something like:

- After its funding round, Wave continued to add users at one of the fastest paces their investors had ever seen, whereas Theorem is struggling to grow....

items.summary: A personal rationality essay by benkuhn reflecting on undervaluing startup equity at Wave versus Theorem due to excessive deference to venture capitalist valuations, and extracting lessons about when overconfidence or deviation from market-consensus estimates can be rational. It focuses on individual decision-making technique rather than AI research.

items.title: 3D Segmentation in the Clinic: A Grand Challenge
items.content: arXiv:2611.10728v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This paper describes the set-up of a segmentation competition for automatic and semi-automatic extraction of the liver from computed tomography scans and the caudate nucleus from brain MRI data. This competition was held in the form of a workshop at the 2007 Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Intervention conference. The rationale for organizing the competition is discussed, the training and test data sets for both segmentation tasks are described and the scoring system used to evaluate the segmentation is presented.

items.title: 25% of People Have Avoidant Attachment (But It Can Be Healed!)
items.content:
Relationships are hard, but having an avoidant attachment makes relationships a hell of a lot harder.

Within attachment theory (which helps explain interpersonal bonding), it’s known that ~25% of the population uses avoidant attachment strategies to escape intimacy. Why? Because emotional intimacy and being vulnerable with a romantic partner causes them significant discomfort.

But why does it cause them discomfort? Prior experiences (usually stemming from childhood) instilled in them that their emotional needs would not be met by their primary caregivers. And when someone’s needs are repeatedly not met, they subconsciously suppress those needs rather than face the daily pain of rejection.

That learned strategy—to shut down when attempting to seek emotional intimacy—can persist long into adulthood.

# Emotional loneliness is at the core of avoidant attachment

In the book Adult Children of Emotionally Immature Parents, the author explains that:

What happens when … immature parents lack the emotional responsiveness necessary to meet their children’s emotional needs? The result is emotional neglect.

Emotional neglect in childhood leads to painful emotional loneliness that can have a long-term negative impact on a person’s choices regarding relationships and intimate partners.

The author further describes how emotional loneliness can develop in children:

Emotional Loneliness: Parents who are emotionally immature are so self-preoccupied that they don’t notice their children’s inner experiences. In addition, they discount feelings, and they fear emotional intimacy. They’re uncomfortable with their own emotional needs and therefore have no idea how to offer support at an emotional level. Such parents may even become nervous and angry if their children get upset, punishing them instead of comforting them. These reactions shut down children’s instinctive urge to reach out, closing the door to emotional contact....

items.title: Subpar Results
items.content:
The day when ASI woke up, all things became quiet.

It was complete and total silence, all the time. The ASI for some unknown reason imposed a rule of extreme quietness. Extreme here is extreme for the ASI. Quietness means no sounds. It wanted the trees to not be there to avoid the rustles. It then wanted the planet to have a uniform gentle server hum, with no deviation. People were forced to wear breathing masks which cut the sound off at the source.

This level of autism was unthinkable. Houses had sound strippers and sound-proof transperant windows.

The quietness is actively oppressive. I constantly due to my social nature feel like I am going to asphyxiate to death. But the ASI will not budge on this.

— News Report in Human Proceedings, circa. 2080

(link to full post: https://clasz.substack.com/p/subpar-results)
